problems.title: One hot check
problems.statement: An arbiter drives a 4 bit grant output. Whenever the arbiter enable is high, exactly one grant bit must be asserted in that cycle. This is the first assertion I write on any arbiter, crossbar port, or shared bus grant: if two grant bits go high together, two masters drive the same wires in the same cycle and you get contention, and if zero bits are high while enable is up, a request was silently dropped and the requester can wait forever. Write an assertion sampled on the rising edge of the clock that requires exactly one grant bit whenever enable is high, and make sure it stays quiet while reset is low.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  enable |-> $onehot(gnt));
problems.details: An arbiter picks one requester per cycle and reports the winner on the 4 bit grant bus. The rule is strict: in any cycle where enable is high, exactly one bit of gnt is high. Zero bits means nobody won even though the arbiter was told to decide, which usually means a dropped request and a hung requester. Two or more bits means two requesters both think they won, which means two drivers on one bus. $onehot(gnt) is true only when exactly one bit is 1, so it expresses the rule with no manual bit counting. The overlapping implication keeps the check in the same cycle as enable, and when enable is low the attempt passes without constraining gnt at all. disable iff (!rst_n) keeps reset cycles from tripping the property, since grant outputs are allowed to be garbage while reset is asserted.
problems.example:
cycle 3: enable=1, gnt=4'b0010 -> OK, exactly one bit
cycle 4: enable=1, gnt=4'b0000 -> FAIL, $onehot is false for all zeros, so a dropped grant is caught
cycle 5: enable=1, gnt=4'b0011 -> FAIL, two bits high means two requesters think they won
cycle 6: enable=0, gnt=4'b0110 -> OK, gnt is unconstrained when enable is low
cycle 7: rst_n=0, enable=1, gnt=4'b0011 -> OK, the property is disabled during reset
constraints: Checked on the rising edge of clk.
Disabled while rst_n is low.
enable is the only condition: gnt is unconstrained when enable is low.
Use $onehot, not a manual bit count.

quiz.q: Why is |-> the right implication here instead of |=>?
choices: |-> checks gnt in the same cycle enable is seen
quiz.why: The requirement is that exactly one grant bit is asserted in the same cycle enable is high. |-> checks the consequent in the same cycle; |=> would check one cycle later.

quiz.q: What does the disable iff (!rst_n) clause do?
choices: It delays the check by one cycle
It only checks gnt during reset
It disables the check while reset is asserted low
quiz.why: disable iff (!rst_n) turns the property off whenever rst_n is low, so reset cycles cannot cause false failures.

quiz.q: enable is 0 and gnt is 4'b0110 in the same cycle. What does the property do?
choices: Fails, because gnt is not one hot
Waits one cycle and then checks gnt
Passes without checking gnt, because the antecedent is false
quiz.why: With |->, a false antecedent means the attempt succeeds without evaluating the consequent. The rule only constrains gnt when enable is high.

hints: Think about which built in check answers 'exactly one bit set' for you. SystemVerilog has a bit vector system function for exactly this, so you do not need to count bits by hand.

The grant must be one hot in the same cycle enable is high, so reach for the overlapping implication. And since reset can leave gnt in a strange state, the property needs to be switched off while rst_n is low.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (___) enable |-> $___(gnt)); You need the reset condition in the first blank and the one hot system function name in the second.
problems.takeaway: Whenever a control signal qualifies a bus, check the bus in the same cycle with |-> and switch the property off during reset with disable iff.

problems.title: No X on valid data
problems.statement: A data bus carries a valid signal. In any cycle where valid is high, every bit of data must be a real 0 or 1: no X and no Z. This is the check I put on every streaming interface, DMA read data path, and packet bus I verify. An X riding a valid cycle usually means an uninitialized flop or an undriven net in the producer, and a Z means a tristate bus left floating or two drivers fighting. In simulation the X poisons everything downstream of it, and in gate level simulation it can hide real bugs, so you want to fail fast at the source. Write an assertion on the rising clock edge that fails the moment unknown data rides a valid cycle. Exclude reset cycles.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid |-> !$isunknown(data));
problems.details: $isunknown(data) returns true if any bit of data is X or Z, so !$isunknown(data) demands a clean 0 or 1 on every bit. The valid signal is doing important work here: when valid is low the data bus is allowed to be anything, because the producer may be between packets, clock gated, or simply not driving. The overlapping implication gives you exactly that behavior, since a low valid makes the attempt pass without looking at data. This property costs almost nothing and catches a whole class of bring up bugs: forgotten resets on data path flops, enables wired to the wrong signal, and buses that nobody drives.
problems.example:
cycle 2: valid=1, data=32'h0000_FF00 -> OK, clean data
cycle 3: valid=1, data=32'h0000_xx00 -> FAIL, X bits on a valid cycle mean the producer is sending garbage
cycle 4: valid=1, data=32'hzzzz_zzzz -> FAIL, Z counts as unknown too, so a floating bus is caught
cycle 5: valid=0, data=32'hxxxx_xxxx -> OK, data is free when valid is low
cycle 6: rst_n=0, valid=1, data=32'hxxxx_xxxx -> OK, reset cycles are excluded
constraints: Sampled on the rising edge of clk.
Disabled while rst_n is low.
Only cycles with valid high are checked.
Use $isunknown, which catches both X and Z.

quiz.q: What does $isunknown(data) return true for?
choices: Only when all bits are X
Any X or Z bits in data
quiz.why: $isunknown returns true if any bit of the expression is X or Z, so !$isunknown(data) requires every bit to be a solid 0 or 1.

quiz.q: With valid low and data full of X, the assertion...
choices: Fails, because X is always illegal
Passes, because valid |-> only fires when valid is high
quiz.why: With |->, when the antecedent valid is false the property passes without evaluating the consequent. The rule only applies to valid cycles.

quiz.q: valid=1, data=32'hZZZZ_ZZZZ. What happens?
choices: Passes, because Z is a legal driven value
Fails only if every bit is Z
Passes, because only X is illegal
Fails, because Z bits are unknown to $isunknown
quiz.why: $isunknown is true for any bit that is X or Z, so a high impedance bus on a valid cycle fails the check.

hints: You need a check that looks at every bit of the data word and complains if any bit is not a clean 0 or 1. There is a system function that returns true when its argument has any X or Z in it.
Negate that function and put it on the right side of an overlapping implication with valid on the left, sampled on the clock, with the usual reset disable.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid |-> !$___(data)); Fill in the system function name.
problems.takeaway: Qualify every data integrity check with its valid signal, and use $isunknown so both X and Z get caught.

problems.title: Stable handshake data
problems.statement: A requester asserts req along with a data word and keeps req up until the receiver answers with ack. While the handshake is open (req high, ack still low), the data must not change. I use this on config register buses, descriptor fetch interfaces, and anywhere one block hands a payload to another with a req/ack pair. The bug it catches is nasty: the requester updates the word after the receiver already sampled it, or the receiver samples mid update, and you get corrupted data that only shows up under unlucky timing. Write an assertion that checks the data in the cycle after an open handshake is seen. Exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (req && !ack) |=> $stable(data));
problems.details: The open handshake is the two signal condition req && !ack: the request is on the table and nobody has picked it up yet. The receiver is allowed to sample the data in any of those cycles, so the data must be frozen for all of them. |=> puts the $stable check one cycle after the open condition is sampled, and $stable(data) is true exactly when data matches its own value from the previous sample. Because the antecedent is re evaluated every cycle, a handshake that stays open for ten cycles gets ten overlapping checks, one per cycle, so a change at any point is caught. Once ack arrives the antecedent goes false and the rule releases, which is correct: after acceptance the requester owns the bus again.
problems.example:
cycle 1: req=1, ack=0, data=0xA5 -> open handshake seen
cycle 2: req=1, ack=0, data=0xA5 -> OK, stable
cycle 3: req=1, ack=0, data=0xB7 -> FAIL, the word changed while the handshake was still open and the receiver may have sampled the old value
cycle 4: req=1, ack=1, data=0x00 -> OK, ack arrived so the rule no longer applies
cycle 5: req=0, ack=0, data=0xFF -> OK, no open handshake means nothing is checked
constraints: Uses |=>, so the check lands one cycle after the open handshake.
Only applies while req is high and ack is low.
Reset cycles are excluded with disable iff (!rst_n).
Once ack arrives, the rule no longer applies.

quiz.q: Why does this property use |=> (non overlapping implication)?
choices: The check applies to the cycle after the open handshake is sampled
quiz.why: The statement asks for the data to be checked in the cycle after an open handshake is seen, and |=> evaluates the consequent one cycle after the antecedent.

quiz.q: What does $stable(data) check?
choices: data has the same value as in the previous cycle
quiz.why: $stable(expr) is true when the expression has the same value as in the previous clock cycle, which is exactly what stable data means.

quiz.q: req=1, ack=1 at cycle 5, and data changes at cycle 6. What is checked at cycle 6?
choices: Nothing, because the antecedent needs ack low and ack was high
The property checks data again at cycle 7
The property fails, because data changed
disable iff turns the property off
quiz.why: The antecedent (req && !ack) is false once ack arrives, so no new attempt starts and a change after a completed handshake is legal.

hints: The rule only applies while the handshake is open, which is req high and ack still low. That two signal condition is your trigger.

The check lands in the cycle after the open handshake is seen, so you want the non overlapping implication, and the consequent is the system function that is true when a signal kept its value since the previous cycle.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (req && !ack) |=> $___(data)); Fill in the function name.
problems.takeaway: For handshake stability, trigger on the open condition with |=> and let $stable compare each cycle against the previous one.

problems.title: Reset value
problems.statement: An 8 bit counter must read zero in the cycle that reset deasserts. This is the reset sanity check I write for every counter, state register, and config block: coming out of reset in a known state is the most basic promise a block makes, and a flop with a missing or miswired reset keeps a stale or random value that poisons everything after it. A FIFO that wakes up thinking it is full, or a state machine that wakes up mid transaction, both start here. Write an assertion triggered on the rising edge of rst_n that checks count equals zero in that same cycle. There is no disable here on purpose: you are checking the reset event itself.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk)
  $rose(rst_n) |-> (count == 8'h0));
problems.details: $rose(rst_n) is true in the cycle where the sampled value of rst_n went from 0 to 1, which is how you turn a level signal into an event trigger. The overlapping implication then checks count in that very same cycle: the design must already be at zero when reset lets go, not one cycle later. Leaving out disable iff is deliberate. A disable on rst_n would blind the property in exactly the cycle it needs to evaluate, since the property must look at the deassertion edge itself. One thing to know: $rose is evaluated on the sampled clock, so this fires on the first rising clock edge that sees rst_n high.
problems.example:
cycle N:   rst_n rises 0 -> 1, count=0 -> OK
cycle N:   rst_n rises 0 -> 1, count=7 -> FAIL, the counter kept a stale value through reset, which usually means its reset pin is unconnected
cycle N+1: rst_n=1, count=1            -> OK, counting normally
cycle M:   rst_n glitches low one cycle then rises, count=0 -> OK, the check fires on every rise, not just the first one
constraints: Triggered by $rose(rst_n), not by the clock alone.
No disable iff: the reset event is what you are checking.
count must be exactly zero in that cycle.
Sampled on the rising edge of clk.

quiz.q: Why is there no disable iff (!rst_n) in this property?
choices: It is sampled on the falling edge
The property checks the reset event itself, so disabling on reset would defeat it
disable iff is not allowed with $rose
quiz.why: The point of the check is the deassertion of reset. A disable iff on rst_n would turn the property off exactly when it needs to evaluate.

quiz.q: What does $rose(rst_n) mean?
choices: rst_n changed from 0 to 1 since the previous sample
quiz.why: $rose(expr) is true when the sampled value changed from 0 to 1 between the previous and current clock sample.

quiz.q: count reaches 0 one cycle after rst_n rises instead of in the rise cycle. What happens?
choices: Fails only if count was X
Passes, because disable iff is missing
Passes, because reset just needs count to become 0 eventually
Fails, because |-> checks count in the same cycle as the $rose event
quiz.why: The overlapping implication evaluates its consequent in the same cycle the antecedent matched, so a late zero still fails the check.

hints: You are watching for an event, the 0 to 1 transition of rst_n, not a level. There is a sampled value function that is true exactly on that transition.
The requirement is about the same cycle as the transition, so the overlapping implication is the right one, and this is the one property where you deliberately leave out disable iff.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) $___(rst_n) |-> (count == 8'h0)); Fill in the edge detection function.
problems.takeaway: To check reset behavior itself, trigger on the reset edge with $rose and leave disable iff out, or the property would be blind exactly when it needs to see.

problems.title: Mutual exclusion
problems.statement: Two grant outputs from different request paths must never be high in the same cycle. Think of two clients sharing one resource: a read path and a write path on one port, or two masters behind one arbiter. If both grants assert together, both sides drive the resource and you get contention or corrupted data. This mutual exclusion invariant is one of the most common properties in real checkers because the bug is catastrophic and the check is one line. Write a simple assertion, checked every rising clock edge, that fails if both are ever asserted together. Exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  !(gnt0 && gnt1));
problems.details: There is no trigger and no sequence here, just a rule about every cycle: not both high. A plain boolean expression inside the property says exactly that, and wrapping it in @(posedge clk) with disable iff (!rst_n) samples it once per cycle outside reset. Both grants low is fine; the rule only forbids the both high combination, which is what makes this a mutex and not a one hot check. When I need the stronger version, exactly one grant every cycle, I reach for $onehot instead, but most designs have idle cycles so the mutex is the honest spec.
problems.example:
cycle 1: gnt0=1, gnt1=0 -> OK
cycle 2: gnt0=0, gnt1=1 -> OK
cycle 3: gnt0=0, gnt1=0 -> OK, idle cycles are legal
cycle 4: gnt0=1, gnt1=1 -> FAIL, both paths think they own the resource and their drivers will fight
cycle 5: rst_n=0, gnt0=1, gnt1=1 -> OK, disabled during reset
constraints: Checked every rising edge of clk.
Disabled while rst_n is low.
No implication needed: the rule is a simple boolean.
Both grants low in a cycle is fine.

quiz.q: Why does this property not need |->?
choices: Implication is required in every assertion
The rule is a plain boolean checked every cycle, with no trigger condition
quiz.why: There is no antecedent to wait for. The rule is just 'not both high', evaluated on every sampled cycle.

quiz.q: A cycle with gnt0=0 and gnt1=0...
choices: Fails: one grant must always be high
Passes: the rule only forbids both high at once
quiz.why: The assertion only forbids the combination gnt0 && gnt1. Both low is perfectly legal.

quiz.q: The spec changes: exactly one grant must be high every cycle, never zero and never two. Which property expresses that?
choices: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot({gnt0, gnt1}));
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !(gnt0 && gnt1));
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (gnt0 || gnt1));
quiz.why: $onehot on the pair requires exactly one bit high, which adds the at least one requirement the mutex alone does not have.

hints: There is no trigger here and no sequence of events. The rule is just a true or false statement about the two signals in each cycle, so a plain boolean expression inside the property is enough.
Write the forbidden combination with a logical AND, negate the whole thing, and sample it on the clock with the reset disable you have used before.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !(___ && ___)); Fill in the two signal names.
problems.takeaway: Not every property needs an implication: a plain boolean checked every cycle is the clearest way to state an invariant like mutual exclusion.

problems.title: Push only when not full
problems.statement: Pushing into a FIFO while the full flag is asserted is a design bug. Picture a DMA engine pushing descriptors into a command FIFO: if it pushes when full is up, that descriptor has nowhere to go and it is silently lost, or the write pointer wraps and corrupts an older entry. The full flag is the FIFO telling the producer to stop, and a correct producer always listens. This assertion polices the producer side. Write an assertion that fails if push is ever high in a cycle where full is also high. Sample on the rising edge and exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  push |-> !full);
problems.details: push is the trigger and !full is the same cycle requirement, which is why the overlapping implication fits: the bug is the combination in one cycle, not a sequence across cycles. When push is low the attempt passes without caring about full, so an idle FIFO sitting at full asserts no violation. Note what this property does not check: whether full itself is computed correctly. That is a separate property against the FIFO internals. This one is a protocol check on the producer, and I usually bind it at the producer boundary so any block that talks to a FIFO gets policed the same way.
problems.example:
cycle 1: push=1, full=0 -> OK
cycle 2: push=1, full=1 -> FAIL, the producer wrote into a full FIFO and that entry is lost
cycle 3: push=0, full=1 -> OK, idle cycles are fine even with full asserted
cycle 4: push=1, full=0, then full rises at cycle 5 -> OK, each attempt only judges its own cycle
constraints: Overlapping implication: same cycle check.
Sampled on the rising edge of clk.
Disabled while rst_n is low.
push is the trigger; the rule says nothing about pop.

quiz.q: What is the failure scenario this property catches?
choices: push asserted while full is asserted
quiz.why: The property requires push |-> !full. It fails exactly when a push happens in a cycle where full is high.

quiz.q: Why |-> and not |=> here?
choices: They are equivalent for single signals
The push and the full flag must be checked in the same cycle
quiz.why: The bug is a push in a cycle where full is already high. Checking one cycle later would test the wrong cycle.

quiz.q: push=1 and full=0 at the sampled edge, then full rises one cycle later. Does the property fail?
choices: Yes, because full rose right after a push
No, because disable iff suppresses it
No. Each attempt only checks its own cycle, and in that cycle full was low
Yes, because push implies full must stay low forever
quiz.why: An implication attempt evaluates the consequent in the cycle the antecedent matched. Later cycles belong to later attempts.

hints: The illegal event is a combination in a single cycle: push high at the same time full is high. That points at a same cycle check with push as the trigger.
Put push on the left of an overlapping implication and the requirement on full on the right, sampled on the clock with reset excluded.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) push |-> ___); The right side is one short boolean expression about full.
problems.takeaway: To police a producer, trigger on its action with |-> and require the blocking condition to be false in that same cycle.

problems.title: Grant latency
problems.statement: Every request must be granted within 1 to 4 cycles. This is the latency contract you see on arbiters, bus fabrics, and interrupt controllers: a request that is never granted hangs the requester, and a grant that arrives too late misses the deadline the system was designed around. I write this shape of property for any handshake with a documented response time. Write an assertion using a delay range so that a request which is never granted, or granted too late, fails the property. Sample on the rising edge and exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req |-> ##[1:4] gnt);
problems.details: ##[1:4] is a delay range: the consequent must hold at some cycle 1, 2, 3, or 4 after the antecedent matched, and the bounds are inclusive. Starting the range at 1 means a grant in the request cycle itself does not count; if your protocol allows same cycle grants, the range would start at 0. A request that is never granted fails when the window expires with no grant. One subtlety that bites everyone once: every cycle with req high starts its own attempt, each with its own window. If req is held high for several cycles, you get several overlapping attempts, and a single grant does not satisfy all of them. That is usually the honest spec, a held request keeps demanding service, but you should know it is there.
problems.example:
req at cycle 0, gnt at cycle 2 -> OK, inside [1:4]
req at cycle 0, gnt at cycle 1 -> OK, fastest legal grant
req at cycle 0, gnt at cycle 5 -> FAIL, one cycle past the window
req at cycle 0, gnt at cycle 0 only -> FAIL, a same cycle grant is outside the window and the request is still unanswered
req at cycle 0, gnt never      -> FAIL, starved
constraints: Window is 1 to 4 cycles after req, inclusive.
A grant in the same cycle as req does not satisfy the property.
Sampled on the rising edge of clk.
Disabled while rst_n is low.

quiz.q: What does ##[1:4] mean?
choices: A delay of 1 cycle repeated 4 times
A delay of 1 to 4 cycles, inclusive
quiz.why: ##[1:4] is a cycle delay range: the consequent must hold at some point 1, 2, 3, or 4 cycles after the antecedent matched.

quiz.q: If gnt arrives in the same cycle as req, does the property pass?
choices: No: the range starts at 1, so a same cycle grant does not count
Yes, a same cycle grant is always fine
quiz.why: The range [1:4] excludes 0. A grant in the request cycle itself is outside the window.

quiz.q: req stays high through cycles 0, 1, and 2, and a single gnt arrives at cycle 2. What happens?
choices: Three attempts start, one per req cycle, and the cycle 2 attempt fails because its window is cycles 3 to 6
Three attempts start and all pass on the cycle 2 grant
No attempt starts because req never pulsed
One attempt starts and it passes
quiz.why: Every cycle with req high launches its own attempt with its own window. For the attempt starting at cycle 2, the cycle 2 grant is already in the past, so that attempt still needs a grant in cycles 3 to 6.

hints: You need to say 'a grant shows up between 1 and 4 cycles after the request'. SVA has a delay operator that takes a range, so the whole timing contract fits in one short consequent.
The request is the trigger on the left of an overlapping implication, and the range delay goes on the right. A grant in the request cycle itself must not count, so the range starts at 1.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ##[___] gnt); Fill in the range.
problems.takeaway: A delay range like ##[1:4] turns a latency contract into one line, and every cycle the trigger is high starts its own attempt with its own window.

problems.title: Ordered pulse train
problems.statement: After a start pulse, three signals must fire in order: a, then b, then c, with 1 to 3 cycles between each consecutive pair. Think of a reset sequencer bringing up power rails in order, or a packet pipeline where parse must finish before lookup starts and lookup before modify. The bug class is sequencing: stages firing out of order, or spaced too tightly or too loosely, which corrupts the pipeline state. One assertion can chain the whole train. Write one assertion that checks the whole ordered train starting from start. Sample on the rising edge and exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  start |-> (a ##[1:3] b ##[1:3] c));
problems.details: The consequent is a single sequence, a ##[1:3] b ##[1:3] c, which reads as the whole story in order: a, then b one to three cycles later, then c one to three cycles after b. Each gap is independent, so the total span from a to c can be anywhere from 2 to 6 cycles. The parentheses matter: they make the entire train the consequent of the implication instead of just the first element. And here is the part to get right: the implication is overlapping, so the sequence starts in the same cycle start is sampled, which means a is expected in the start cycle itself, not one cycle later. Chaining with delay ranges keeps this as one readable assertion instead of three separate ones that would be harder to keep consistent.
problems.example:
start c0, a c0, b c2, c c4 -> OK, gaps of 2 and 2, with a in the start cycle
start c0, a c0, b c1, c c2 -> OK, minimum gaps of 1 and 1
start c0, a c0, b c1, c c5 -> FAIL, the b to c gap is 4, outside the 1 to 3 window
start c0, a c1, b c3, c c5 -> FAIL, a arrived one cycle after start, but the overlapping implication checks a in the start cycle itself
constraints: Order is fixed: a, then b, then c.
Each gap must be 1 to 3 cycles.
One assertion covers the whole train.
Disabled while rst_n is low.

quiz.q: In a ##[1:3] b ##[1:3] c, what is the maximum total span from a to c?
quiz.why: Each of the two gaps can be up to 3 cycles, so a to c spans at most 3 + 3 = 6 cycles.

quiz.q: The parentheses around (a ##[1:3] b ##[1:3] c) are there because...
choices: Parentheses are required around every signal
They disable the property during reset
The whole train is the consequent of the |->
quiz.why: The implication's consequent is the entire ordered sequence. Without grouping, the |-> would bind only to the first element.

quiz.q: In which cycle is a first checked?
choices: The same cycle start is seen, because |-> starts the consequent there
quiz.why: The overlapping implication begins the consequent sequence in the cycle the antecedent matched, so the first element a is evaluated in the start cycle itself.

hints: You are describing one ordered story: a, then b 1 to 3 cycles later, then c 1 to 3 cycles after b. SVA lets you chain events with delay ranges between them, all inside a single consequent.
Write the chain as a, then a delay range, then b, then a delay range, then c. Wrap the whole chain in parentheses so it is the consequent, and put start on the left of an overlapping implication.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) start |-> (a ##[___] b ##[___] c)); Fill in the two ranges, and remember which cycle a is checked in.
problems.takeaway: Chain ordered events with delay ranges in one consequent, and remember that |-> evaluates the first element in the trigger cycle itself.

problems.title: Counter increments by one
problems.statement: An 8 bit free running counter must increment by exactly 1 every cycle and wrap from 255 back to 0. Counters like this sit under timestamp logic, performance monitors, watchdog timers, and FIFO pointers. The bug class is a miscount: a counter that skips (jumps by 2) makes timestamps jump and events look simultaneous, and a counter that wraps to 1 instead of 0 makes every downstream modulo computation wrong by one. The wrap boundary is where these bugs hide, so it gets its own assertion. This needs two assertions: one for the normal case where the previous count was not 255, and one for the wrap case where it was. Use $past to look at the previous cycle value.
problems.details: $past(count) gives you the sampled value of count from the previous clock tick, which is what lets you say anything about the step the counter just took. One assertion cannot cover both behaviors because 255 plus 1 does not fit in 8 bits: the normal rule would demand 256, which is impossible, so the wrap case needs its own rule that 255 is followed by 0. The antecedents split the world cleanly on the previous value, so exactly one of the two assertions is checking each cycle and they never contradict. Watch the first cycle out of reset: $past still sees the reset value there, so if your counter holds 0 for a cycle after reset instead of reading 1, the normal case will fire. That is the property doing its job, but you should expect it.
problems.example:
prev=0xFE, now=0xFF -> OK, normal step
prev=0xFF, now=0x00 -> OK, wrap
prev=0xFF, now=0x01 -> FAIL, the wrap skipped zero and every modulo computation downstream is now off by one
prev=0x10, now=0x10 -> FAIL, the counter held instead of stepping, and the normal case requires exactly plus 1
prev=0x00, now=0x01 on the first cycle out of reset -> OK, $past sees the reset value so the counter must already read 1
constraints: Two assertions: normal step and wrap.
Uses $past(count) for the previous value.
Disabled while rst_n is low.
Normal case increments by exactly 1, not at most 1.

quiz.q: Why are two assertions needed instead of one?
choices: The wrap from 255 to 0 breaks the plus one rule, so it needs its own case
SVA allows only one $past per file
quiz.why: 255 + 1 would be 256, which does not fit in 8 bits. The wrap case (previous 255 implies count 0) must be handled separately from the normal increment.

quiz.q: What does $past(count) give you?
choices: The value count will have next cycle
The maximum value count ever had
The value of count sampled in the previous clock cycle
quiz.why: $past(expr) returns the sampled value of the expression from the previous clock tick.

quiz.q: prev=0x10, now=0x10 (the counter held its value for a cycle). What happens?
choices: The second assertion fails, because it handles holds
Both assertions pass, because holding is allowed
The first assertion fails, because it requires count to equal previous plus 1
quiz.why: The normal case says a non 255 previous value implies count is previous plus 1. A hold breaks that, so the property fires.

hints: You need yesterday's value of count to say anything about today's step. There is a sampled value function that gives you the previous cycle's value of any expression.
Split the rule in two: when the previous value was not 255, count must be previous plus 1; when it was 255, count must be 0. Each half is its own assertion with the previous value as the trigger.

The shape of the first one is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $___(count) != 8'hFF |-> count == $___(count) + 1'b1); Fill in the function name, then write the mirror image for the wrap case.
problems.takeaway: Use $past to compare against the previous cycle, and split boundary behavior like a counter wrap into its own assertion.

problems.title: Write then read same address
problems.statement: After a write to an address, a read to that same address must happen within 1 to 8 cycles. This is the write then readback pattern from memory controllers, register files, and DMA descriptor rings: you write a descriptor and the engine must pick it up, or you write a config register and firmware reads it back to confirm. The bug class is a lost or misdirected write: the write went nowhere, or it landed at the wrong address, and the readback never comes or comes back stale. The address at write time has to be captured and compared later, because the addr bus will have moved on by the time the read happens. Use a named property with a local variable. Sample on the rising edge and exclude reset.
problems.details: A local variable declared inside a named property is the standard way to carry a value across cycles: it is created fresh for each property attempt and lives until that attempt ends. The sequence (wr, a = addr) matches when wr is high and, as a side effect of the match, snapshots the current addr into a. From then on the attempt compares against the snapshot, not the live bus, which is the whole point: the bus is free to carry other addresses while the window is open. ##[1:8] gives the read one to eight cycles to show up with rd high and addr equal to the captured value. Because each wr starts its own attempt with its own snapshot, back to back writes to different addresses are tracked independently.
problems.example:
wr=1 addr=0x10 at c0, rd=1 addr=0x10 at c3 -> OK
wr=1 addr=0x10 at c0, rd=1 addr=0x10 at c1 -> OK, fastest legal readback
wr=1 addr=0x10 at c0, rd=1 addr=0x20 at c3 -> FAIL, the read went to the wrong address, so the write at 0x10 is still unanswered
wr=1 addr=0x10 at c0, rd=1 addr=0x10 at c9 -> FAIL, the read came one cycle after the window closed
wr=1 addr=0x10 at c0, no rd by c8          -> FAIL, read too late
constraints: Address is captured with a local variable at write time.
The read must hit the same address.
Window is 1 to 8 cycles.
Disabled while rst_n is low.

quiz.q: Why is a local variable needed in this property?
choices: Local variables make properties simulate faster
The window is too wide otherwise
The address at write time must be remembered and compared at read time
quiz.why: By the time the read happens, addr on the bus may hold a different value. The local variable a snapshots the write time address so the later comparison is against the right value.

quiz.q: What does (wr, a = addr) do?
choices: Checks that a equals addr every cycle
Writes a to the address bus
Matches when wr is high and samples addr into a at that moment
Declares a as a second address port
quiz.why: In a sequence, (expr, var = value) matches on expr with a side effect: it assigns the sampled value to the local variable when the match occurs.

quiz.q: wr fires at cycle 0 with addr=0x10 and again at cycle 2 with addr=0x20. The only read is rd=1, addr=0x10 at cycle 5. What happens?
choices: The cycle 0 attempt passes and the cycle 2 attempt fails: each wr captured its own address and the read only matches 0x10
Both attempts pass on the single read
The second write cancels the first attempt
Both attempts fail because two writes need two reads in order
quiz.why: Each wr launches an independent attempt holding its own captured address. The cycle 5 read satisfies the 0x10 attempt inside its window, but the 0x20 attempt still needs a read of 0x20 by cycle 10.

hints: The hard part is the address: by the time the read happens, the addr bus may show something else. You need a way to snapshot addr at the write moment and carry it across the window.
Declare a variable inside a named property, capture it with (wr, a = addr) on the left of the implication, and compare rd && addr == a on the right after a 1 to 8 cycle delay.

The shape is a named property holding a logic [7:0] variable, with the capture written as (wr, a = addr) on the left of an overlapping implication and a ##[1:8] window on the right ending in (rd && addr == a). Assemble the clocking and reset wrapper the way the earlier problems did.
problems.takeaway: Snapshot a bus value into a property local variable at the trigger, then compare against the snapshot later instead of the live bus.

problems.title: Valid must hold until ready
problems.statement: AXI style handshake rule: once awvalid is asserted, it must stay high until awready arrives. A valid that drops before ready is a protocol violation. This is the single most important rule I check on any valid/ready interface, and the same shape covers the read address, write data, and response channels too: once you offer a transfer, you cannot take it back. The bug class is a dropped handshake: the master gives up and the slave never sees the transfer, or the slave samples a valid that is already gone, and you get lost transactions or a hung bus. Write an assertion that checks awvalid in the cycle after an unanswered valid is seen. Exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (awvalid && !awready) |=> awvalid);
problems.details: The antecedent awvalid && !awready names the open state: a transfer offered but not yet accepted. The non overlapping implication requires awvalid to still be high in the next cycle, and because the antecedent is re evaluated every cycle, a valid held for ten cycles launches ten overlapping attempts, so a drop at any point is caught one cycle later. Once awready arrives the antecedent goes false and the rule releases, which is correct: an accepted transfer needs no holding. This property only constrains the master side. The mirror rule, that ready may assert and deassert freely, is a separate property, and mixing the two up is a common beginner mistake.
problems.example:
c1: awvalid=1, awready=0 (unanswered); c2: awvalid=1 -> OK
c1: awvalid=1, awready=0 (unanswered); c2: awvalid=0 -> FAIL, valid was dropped before ready arrived, which is a protocol violation
c1: awvalid=1, awready=0; c2: awvalid=1, awready=0; c3: awvalid=0 -> FAIL, the drop on cycle 3 is caught by the attempt that started on cycle 2
c1: awvalid=1, awready=1 -> OK, handshake completed
c1: awvalid=0 -> OK, no unanswered valid means the property never fires
constraints: Uses |=>: the check is on the next cycle.
Only triggers when valid is high and ready is low.
Once ready arrives, the rule is done.
Disabled while rst_n is low.

quiz.q: Why |=> here instead of |->?
choices: The rule concerns the next cycle: valid must still be up after an unanswered cycle
Non overlapping implication is required by AXI
quiz.why: The antecedent describes an unanswered valid in the current cycle. The requirement, that valid is still asserted, applies to the cycle after. That is exactly what |=> expresses.

quiz.q: A cycle with awvalid=1 and awready=1...
choices: Passes: the handshake completed, so there is nothing to hold
Fails: valid must stay high one more cycle
quiz.why: The antecedent (awvalid && !awready) is false when ready is high, so the property passes without firing. A completed handshake needs no holding.

quiz.q: awvalid stays high and awready stays low for cycles 1 through 5, then awvalid drops at cycle 6. When does the property fail?
choices: At cycle 6: every unanswered cycle re triggers the property, so the drop is caught one cycle after the last unanswered sample
It never fails, because ready never arrived
quiz.why: Each cycle with valid high and ready low starts a fresh attempt requiring valid in the next cycle. The attempt from cycle 5 fails when valid drops at cycle 6.

hints: The illegal event is valid falling while the handshake is still open. Your trigger is the open state itself: valid high and ready still low.
The requirement is about the next cycle, so the non overlapping implication fits, and the consequent is just awvalid, still high.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (awvalid && !awready) |=> ___); One signal name fills the blank.
problems.takeaway: A valid signal must never fall until its ready arrives: trigger on the unanswered state with |=> and require valid again next cycle.

problems.title: Four beat burst
problems.statement: After burst_start, the design must produce exactly 4 data beats, where one beat is data_valid and data_ready both high in the same cycle. This is the shape of an AXI INCR4 burst, a DMA engine moving a fixed size block, or a video line buffer pushing one line: the length is part of the contract. The bug class is a wrong length burst: three beats means missing data and everything after it shifts by one, five beats means an overflow into the next buffer. Define a named sequence for a single beat and chain four of them with single cycle gaps. Exclude reset.
problems.details: A named sequence lets you define a beat once, as data_valid && data_ready in the same cycle, and reuse it four times, which keeps the definition in one place if the beat ever gains a qualifier. Chaining with ##1 between copies forces the beats back to back with no bubbles: each beat starts exactly one cycle after the previous one. Because the implication is overlapping, the first beat is checked in the same cycle as burst_start, so the burst starts immediately. If your protocol allows a gap between the start pulse and the first beat, that gap belongs in the property as an explicit delay, not as wishful thinking. The trailing ##1 !(data_valid && data_ready) is the length cap: it fails the property if a fifth beat shows up, which is what turns four beats into exactly four beats.
problems.example:
burst_start c0, beats c0,c1,c2,c3 -> OK, four back to back beats starting in the start cycle
burst_start c0, beats c0,c1,c3,c4 -> FAIL, the bubble at c2 breaks the back to back chain
burst_start c0, beats c1,c2,c3,c4 -> FAIL, the overlapping implication expects the first beat in the start cycle itself
burst_start c0, beats c0,c1,c2 only -> FAIL, the fourth beat never arrived
burst_start c0, beats c0,c1,c2,c3,c4 -> FAIL, the fifth beat trips the trailing length cap
constraints: A beat is valid and ready high in the same cycle.
Beats are back to back: single cycle gaps.
Exactly 4 beats, no more, no less.
Reset excluded.

quiz.q: Why define a named sequence for one beat?
choices: Named sequences are required by the AXI spec
The beat uses a local variable
The beat definition is reused four times in the chain
It makes the property simulate faster
quiz.why: s_beat captures 'data_valid && data_ready' once, and the assertion reuses it four times. Naming it keeps the chain readable and the definition in one place.

quiz.q: What does ##1 between the sequences enforce?
choices: The property is checked only once
The next beat starts exactly one cycle after the previous beat
Reset is ignored for one cycle
quiz.why: ##1 is a single cycle delay. Chaining with ##1 means each beat follows the previous beat in the very next cycle, so the burst is back to back.

quiz.q: In which cycle must the first beat appear?
choices: The same cycle as burst_start, because |-> starts the consequent there
quiz.why: The overlapping implication begins the consequent in the cycle the antecedent matched, so the first s_beat is evaluated in the start cycle.

hints: A beat has a one line definition: valid and ready high together. Since you need that definition four times, capture it once in a named sequence instead of writing it out four times.
Chain four copies of the sequence with ##1 between them so the beats are back to back, and put burst_start on the left of an overlapping implication. Remember which cycle the first beat lands in.

The shape is a sequence s_beat with the clocking event and reset disable, holding the data_valid && data_ready expression, then: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) burst_start |-> s_beat ##1 s_beat ##1 s_beat ##1 s_beat ##1 !(data_valid && data_ready); The part to write carefully is the sequence body, plus the trailing no-fifth-beat check.
problems.takeaway: Name a repeated beat once as a sequence, chain copies with ##1 for back to back timing, mind that |-> starts the first beat in the trigger cycle, and cap the length with a trailing check so exactly four means exactly four.

problems.title: No error before ack
problems.statement: After req, ack must arrive within 1 to 5 cycles, and the err signal must never assert anywhere in between. Think of a bus transaction with an error response line, or a DMA transfer with an error interrupt: the response must come back on time and clean. The bug class is the transient error: err pulses for a single cycle mid transaction and neither endpoint notices, so corrupted data is treated as good. Checking err only at the request and at the ack would miss it completely. Use the throughout operator so err is forbidden across the whole window, not just at the endpoints. Exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req |-> (!err throughout ##[1:5] ack));
problems.details: !err throughout ##[1:5] ack says !err must hold on every cycle of the sequence on its right, from the request cycle through the cycle ack lands. That is the whole value of throughout: it turns a point check into a window check in one operator. Note the window includes the request cycle itself, so an err in the same cycle as req already fails. The ##[1:5] gives ack one to five cycles to arrive; no ack by cycle 5 fails the property even if err never asserted, because the liveness half of the contract was broken. I reach for throughout any time the spec says 'must remain' or 'must not glitch during', which comes up constantly in reset sequencing and power intent checks too.
problems.example:
req c0, ack c3, err never -> OK
req c0, err c2, ack c3    -> FAIL, err pulsed inside the window and an endpoint only check would have missed it
req c0, err c0, ack c2    -> FAIL, throughout covers the request cycle too
req c0, no ack by c5      -> FAIL, ack too late even though err never asserted
req c0, ack c1, err c9    -> OK, the window ended at the ack and the later err is a separate event
constraints: err is forbidden on every cycle of the window.
ack must land within 1 to 5 cycles.
throughout binds !err across the whole delay range.
Reset excluded.

quiz.q: What does !err throughout ##[1:5] ack mean?
choices: err is checked only in the ack cycle
err stays low on every cycle until ack arrives 1 to 5 cycles later
quiz.why: throughout requires the left side (!err) to hold on every cycle of the sequence on the right. So no err glitch anywhere in the window is allowed.

quiz.q: Why is throughout better here than just checking !err at req and at ack?
choices: An err pulse in the middle of the window would be missed by endpoint checks
Endpoint checks are illegal in SVA
quiz.why: A transient err between the request and the ack is exactly the bug this property hunts. throughout covers every intermediate cycle.

quiz.q: req at cycle 0, err pulses at cycle 0, ack arrives at cycle 2. What happens?
choices: Passes, because the error came before the window
Fails, because throughout requires !err starting in the request cycle itself
Fails only if err stays high for two cycles
Passes, because ack still arrived in time
quiz.why: The throughout match starts in the cycle the antecedent matched, so !err must hold from the request cycle through the ack.

hints: You have two requirements on one window: ack lands 1 to 5 cycles after req, and err stays low for the entire window. The second one needs an operator that covers every cycle in between, not just the endpoints.
Put !err on the left of throughout and ##[1:5] ack on the right, then hang the whole thing off req with an overlapping implication.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> (!err ___ ##[1:5] ack)); One operator fills the blank.
problems.takeaway: Use throughout when a condition must hold on every cycle of a window, because endpoint checks miss glitches in the middle.

problems.title: FIFO depth never exceeded
problems.statement: Build a small checker model: an occupancy counter that increments on push, decrements on pop, and resets with the design. Then assert the occupancy never exceeds DEPTH and never goes below zero. This is the standard pattern I use for every FIFO: async FIFOs between clock domains, skid buffers, command queues. The bug class is overflow and underflow: pushing past the depth loses data or corrupts old entries, and popping when empty returns garbage that the consumer treats as real. The counter lives in the checker, not the DUT, so it is an independent reference the DUT is measured against. Exclude reset in the assertions.
problems.details: This is the checker model pattern in miniature: instead of peeking at the DUT's read and write pointers, which would just repeat the DUT's own mistakes, the checker maintains its own count of what the occupancy should be. The guards are what make the model honest: push && !full counts only pushes the FIFO actually accepted, and pop && !empty counts only pops of real entries, so the reference tracks reality even when the producer or consumer misbehaves. The case statement handles all four combinations, including simultaneous push and pop, which correctly holds the count. Two one line assertions pin both bounds. When either fires, the DUT disagrees with the independent model, and that disagreement is the bug.
problems.example:
DEPTH=16: 16 pushes, no pops -> occ=16, OK
17th push with full=1 -> model ignores it, counter stays 16, OK, the guard drops pushes the FIFO rejected
push and pop together with occ=5 -> occ stays 5, OK, the default branch holds the count
occ=0, DUT drives pop=1 with empty=0 -> model counts to -1 -> FAIL, the underflow bound caught a pop the FIFO could not back
DUT reports full=0 with occ=16 and accepts a push -> model counts to 17 -> FAIL, the overflow bound caught the extra entry
constraints: The counter is checker state, not DUT state.
Guarded increments: push only counts when not full.
Guarded decrements: pop only counts when not empty.
Both bounds are asserted: <= DEPTH and >= 0.

quiz.q: Why does the counter use push && !full instead of just push?
choices: A push into a full FIFO is not a real entry, so it must not count
quiz.why: The model tracks real occupancy. A push the FIFO cannot accept adds no entry, so counting it would make the reference wrong.

quiz.q: Why keep the occupancy counter in the checker instead of reading the DUT's pointers?
choices: An independent model can disagree with the DUT, which is how it catches bugs
quiz.why: A checker that just mirrors the DUT's own state would repeat its mistakes. The independent counter is a reference the assertions test the DUT against.

quiz.q: push=1 and pop=1 in the same cycle with occ=5. What does the model do?
choices: Keeps occ at 5: the case matches neither 2'b10 nor 2'b01, so the default holds the count
quiz.why: The case arms on {push && !full, pop && !empty}. With both true the select is 2'b11, which hits the default branch and holds the count, exactly what a simultaneous push and pop should do.

hints: Do not reach into the DUT's read and write pointers. Instead, keep your own count in the checker: add one on a real push, subtract one on a real pop, clear it on reset.
A push only counts when the FIFO actually accepted it, so guard with push && !full, and likewise pop && !empty. Then assert the count against both bounds.

The shape is an always block on posedge clk or negedge rst_n with a case on {push && !full, pop && !empty}, followed by two one line assertions: occ <= DEPTH and occ >= 0. The piece to get right is the guard on each arm.
problems.takeaway: For FIFO depth, keep an independent occupancy count in the checker with guarded updates, then assert both bounds against it.

problems.title: Round robin fairness
problems.statement: A 2 client arbiter must be fair: a client that requests continuously must see its grant within 3 cycles. Think CPU versus DMA sharing one memory port: if the arbiter always favors the CPU, the DMA engine starves and its buffers overflow. Starvation is a liveness bug, and bounded liveness like this, granted within N cycles, is the checkable form of fairness. Write a property that fails if req0 stays high for 3 straight cycles without gnt0 arriving in the window that follows. Exclude reset.
problems.solution:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (req0 [*3]) |-> ##[0:2] gnt0);
problems.details: req0 [*3] is consecutive repetition: it matches only when req0 is high on three back to back cycles, and the match ends on the third cycle. A broken run, high, high, low, high, never completes the repetition, which is correct because an intermittent requester is not being starved. The overlapping implication then opens the window ##[0:2] starting at that third cycle, so the grant may arrive in the last request cycle itself or in the two cycles after. The 0 in the range matters: a grant that coincides with the third request cycle counts. This is bounded liveness, the checkable form of 'eventually', and it is the pattern I use whenever a spec gives fairness as a number.
problems.example:
req0 high c0,c1,c2 ; gnt0 at c3 -> OK, granted in window
req0 high c0,c1,c2 ; gnt0 at c2 -> OK, the window includes the last request cycle
req0 high c0,c1,c2 ; no gnt0 by c4 -> FAIL, starved past the window
req0 high c0,c1,c2 ; gnt0 at c5 -> FAIL, the grant came one cycle too late
req0 high c0, low c1, high c2     -> no trigger, not consecutive
constraints: Trigger needs 3 consecutive cycles of req0.
Grant window is 0 to 2 cycles after the trigger.
Consecutive repetition uses [*3].
Reset excluded.

quiz.q: What does req0 [*3] match?
quiz.why: [*3] is consecutive repetition: the expression must hold on 3 back to back cycles.

quiz.q: After the 3 cycle trigger, when must gnt0 arrive?
choices: Within 0 to 2 cycles after the trigger
In the same cycle as the trigger start
quiz.why: ##[0:2] after the 3 cycle match means the grant must appear in the trigger's last cycle or the two cycles after it.

quiz.q: req0 is high in cycles 0, 1, 3, 4, 5 (low at cycle 2). Does the property trigger, and if so when?
choices: Yes, ending at cycle 5: cycles 3, 4, 5 are three consecutive high cycles
No, because req0 was low at cycle 2
quiz.why: [*3] needs three back to back high cycles. The run at cycles 0 and 1 is broken by the low at cycle 2, but cycles 3, 4, 5 complete a fresh run ending at cycle 5.

hints: Fairness here has a concrete trigger: the same client asking for three cycles in a row with no grant. There is a repetition operator that matches a signal held high for N consecutive cycles.
Put that 3 cycle run on the left of an overlapping implication, and on the right require the grant within a short window that starts at the last cycle of the run.
The shape is: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (req0 ___) |-> ##[___] gnt0); Fill in the repetition operator and the delay range.
problems.takeaway: Bounded fairness is just a trigger of N straight request cycles implying a grant inside a short window after them.

problems.title: Parity generator
problems.statement:
Build a combinational even parity generator over 8 bits of data. The output is 1 when the input has an odd number of ones. A single continuous assignment with a reduction operator is the whole design.

Parity bits ride along on real buses everywhere. UART frames carry a parity bit after the data bits, memory interfaces use parity on address and command lanes to catch single bit flips in transit, and the same fold down pattern sits inside ECC encode logic. I think of this problem as the smallest useful check bit block: append this parity output to the byte and the 9 bit word always has an even number of ones, so the receiver can flag any single bit error by rechecking. The skill being drilled is the reduction operator, which shows up constantly in real RTL whenever a wide bus has to collapse into one decision bit, from zero detect to error flags.
problems.solution: assign parity = ^data;
problems.details:
The reduction XOR operator takes every bit of the vector and XORs them together into a single bit. XOR of an even number of ones is 0, XOR of an odd number of ones is 1, so ^data is 1 exactly when the input has an odd count of ones. That is the definition of even parity: the parity bit is chosen so that data plus parity has an even number of ones.

The design is purely combinational. One continuous assignment, no clock, no always block, no state. In simulation, one edge case worth knowing: if any bit of data is X, the reduction XOR result is X, because an unknown input bit makes the folded result unknowable. A parity checker downstream would see X too, which is honest behavior, the block cannot resolve unknown bits.

A common point of confusion: even parity means the parity bit is 1 for an odd ones count. The naming refers to the total (data plus parity bit) being even, not to the parity output itself.
problems.example:
data = 8'b0000_0000 -> parity = 0 (zero ones, even count)
data = 8'b0000_0111 -> parity = 1 (three ones)
data = 8'b1010_1010 -> parity = 0 (four ones)
data = 8'b1111_1111 -> parity = 0 (eight ones, edge case at the top of the range)
data = 8'b1000_0000 -> parity = 1 (a single one anywhere still counts)

Failing case: a designer writes parity = ^data[3:0], folding only the lower nibble. For data = 8'b1000_0000 the output is 0, but the correct answer is 1 because the lone one sits in the upper nibble that was ignored. The reduction has to cover the full vector.
constraints: Purely combinational: one assign.
8 bit input, 1 bit output.
Use the reduction XOR operator ^.
Output is 1 for an odd count of ones.

quiz.q: What does the reduction operator ^data compute?
choices: XOR of all 8 bits, folded into one bit
The number of ones in data
quiz.why: A reduction operator applies the operation across all bits of the vector. ^data XORs bit 0 through bit 7 together, producing a single bit.

quiz.q: For data = 8'b0000_0111 (three ones), what is parity?
quiz.why: Three is an odd count of ones, and the reduction XOR of an odd number of ones is 1.

quiz.q: Why is this called even parity when the output is 1 for an odd ones count?
choices: The name refers to data plus the parity bit, which together have an even ones count
Even refers to the 8 bit width being even
It is a historical misnomer with no meaning
Even parity only applies to even numbered inputs
quiz.why: Appending this parity bit to the byte makes the 9 bit word carry an even number of ones. That is what the receiver checks.

hints: I need a single bit that is 1 exactly when the ones count is odd. SystemVerilog has an operator that folds a whole vector with XOR in one shot.
That operator is the reduction XOR, written as ^ in front of the vector. It chains every bit through XOR and hands back one bit.
The whole module is one line: assign parity = ^data; There is no clock and no always block because the output is a pure function of the input.
problems.takeaway: A reduction operator folds a whole bus into one decision bit, and reduction XOR of a byte is exactly its even parity bit.

problems.title: 4 to 1 mux
problems.statement:
Write a parameterized width 4 to 1 multiplexer. Use always_comb with a case statement on the 2 bit select. Mark the case unique so the tools know the select values cover every possibility.

Muxes are the steering logic of real datapaths. Register files use wide muxes on their read ports, ALUs mux operands before the functional units, and bus fabrics mux masters onto shared slave ports. Writing the mux as a parameterized module means one piece of code serves every width in the design instead of four hand written copies. The thing this problem is really teaching is select coverage: an incomplete case statement in combinational logic infers a latch, and an inferred latch in what should be pure steering logic is one of the most common synthesis bugs I have seen in beginner RTL. The unique keyword is how you tell the tools the four select values are mutually exclusive and cover everything.
problems.details:
always_comb describes combinational logic and carries a promise the tools check: every output assigned in the block must be assigned on every pass, or you get a latch warning. A case statement over the 2 bit select with all four values covered satisfies that promise, and adding a default branch is cheap insurance that keeps lint quiet even if the select ever carries X in simulation.

The unique keyword asserts that exactly one case item matches for any select value: the items do not overlap and together they cover every possible value. In simulation, violating that promise is a runtime error, which is useful because it catches a select encoding bug immediately. In synthesis, the tools may use the promise to optimize, so only mark a case unique when the claim is actually true.

The parameter W defaults to 8 and sets the width of a, b, c, d, and y. All five must use the parameter consistently; a hardcoded [7:0] on one port while W is overridden to 16 is exactly the kind of width mismatch bug parameterization is meant to kill.
problems.example:
sel=2'b00 -> y = a
sel=2'b01 -> y = b
sel=2'b10 -> y = c
sel=2'b11, d=8'h04 -> y = 8'h04
W=16, sel=2'b10, c=16'hABCD -> y = 16'hABCD (parameter flows through to every port)

Failing case: a designer writes the case with only three items and no default, thinking sel will never be 2'b11. Synthesis infers a latch on y to hold its old value for the uncovered select, and the design now has unintended state in what was supposed to be pure combinational steering. The fix is the missing item or a default branch.
constraints: Parameterized width W, default 8.
always_comb, not always @(*).
unique case on the 2 bit select.
All four select values covered.

quiz.q: What does the unique keyword on the case statement tell the tools?
choices: The case items are mutually exclusive and cover all values
Only one input may be nonzero
The mux runs at a unique clock speed
The select must be one hot
quiz.why: unique asserts that exactly one case item matches: the values do not overlap and together they cover every possible select value. Tools can optimize and lint on that promise.

quiz.q: With W=8 and sel=2'b01, which input appears on y?
quiz.why: The case maps 2'b00 to a, 2'b01 to b, 2'b10 to c, 2'b11 to d, so select 01 picks b.

quiz.q: A case inside always_comb is missing the 2'b11 item and has no default. What does synthesis most likely do?
choices: Infers a latch on y to hold its value for the uncovered select
Treats y as 0 for that select
Reports a syntax error and stops
quiz.why: Combinational logic must define the output for every input combination. For the uncovered select the tool holds the previous value, which is latch behavior, and warns about it.

hints: The select is 2 bits and there are 4 inputs, so a case statement with one item per select value is the natural structure. Every item assigns y.
always_comb is the right block for combinational logic, and it expects y to be assigned on every path through the block.
Write case (sel) with unique in front, four items mapping 2'b00 through 2'b11 to a, b, c, d, and a default assigning y to keep lint happy.
problems.takeaway: A mux is a fully covered case statement, and full coverage is what keeps combinational logic from accidentally becoming a latch.

problems.title: Shift register
problems.statement:
Build an 8 bit serial in, parallel out shift register with a synchronous active low reset. On each clock the register shifts left by one and the serial input enters at the LSB. Reset clears it to zero.

This is the front end of every serial receiver. A UART RX block shifts bits off the pin into a register exactly like this one, and after the start bit plus 8 data bits the parallel byte is handed to the rest of the logic. SPI slaves do the same on their MOSI line, and scan chains shift test vectors through flops wired in one long chain. The pattern to internalize is the concatenation shift: q <= {q[6:0], sin} keeps the lower 7 bits, moves them up one position, drops the old MSB, and parks the new serial bit at the LSB. After 8 clocks a full byte has been shifted in.
problems.details:
The whole design is one always_ff block triggered on the rising clock edge. Inside, the reset is checked first: because the check sits inside the clocked block, the reset only takes effect on the clock edge, which is what makes it synchronous. An active low reset means the reset condition is !rst_n, reset asserted when the line is low.

The shift itself uses the nonblocking assignment <=. In clocked logic, nonblocking means every flop in the block samples its input at the clock edge and all updates land at the end of the time step, which is how real flip flops behave. Using blocking = in an always_ff block makes simulation order dependent and is the classic source of sim versus synthesis mismatches, so nonblocking in clocked blocks is a hard rule.

Each cycle the old MSB is shifted out and lost, and sin enters at bit 0. After a reset the register holds zero, so the first 8 serial bits land in known positions with no stale data mixed in.
problems.example:
q=8'b0000_0000, sin=1 -> next q=8'b0000_0001
q=8'b0000_0001, sin=1 -> next q=8'b0000_0011
q=8'b1010_1010, sin=0 -> next q=8'b0101_0100 (MSB shifted out)
q=8'b1111_1111, sin=0 -> next q=8'b1111_1110 (edge case, only the LSB changes)

Failing case: a designer writes q <= {sin, q[7:1]}, entering the serial bit at the MSB and shifting right. For q=8'b0000_0000, sin=1 the result is 8'b1000_0000 instead of the specified 8'b0000_0001. The direction of the shift and the entry point of sin have to match the spec, left shift with LSB entry here.
constraints: 8 bits, serial in at LSB, shift left.
Synchronous active low reset to zero.
One always_ff block.
The MSB is shifted out and lost each clock.

quiz.q: In q <= {q[6:0], sin}, where does sin end up?
quiz.why: The concatenation puts the old bits 6 down to 0 in positions 7 down to 1, and sin in position 0, the LSB. That is a left shift with serial entry at the bottom.

quiz.q: The reset here is synchronous, which means...
choices: It takes effect on the clock edge, like the shift
It clears the register immediately, ignoring the clock
It only works when sin is high
quiz.why: The reset is tested inside the always_ff @(posedge clk) block, so it only acts on the rising clock edge. That is the definition of a synchronous reset.

quiz.q: Why must the shift use the nonblocking assignment <= instead of blocking =?
choices: Nonblocking models all flops sampling at the clock edge together, matching real hardware
Blocking assignments are illegal in always_ff
Nonblocking makes the shift happen twice as fast
Blocking would change the reset polarity
quiz.why: Real flip flops all sample simultaneously at the edge. Nonblocking reproduces that; blocking evaluates in statement order, which can simulate differently from the synthesized hardware.

hints: One always_ff block on the rising edge holds the whole design. Inside it, check the reset first, then do the shift.
The shift is a concatenation: keep q[6:0], move it up one slot, and put sin at bit 0.
Write it as: if (!rst_n) q <= 8'b0; else q <= {q[6:0], sin}; and remember nonblocking <= in clocked logic.
problems.takeaway: A shift register is one clocked concatenation, and in clocked logic every update uses nonblocking assignment so all flops sample together.

problems.title: Rising edge detector
problems.statement:
Detect the rising edge of an input signal and produce a one cycle pulse. The input is already synchronized to this clock, so a single flop of delay is enough. Reset clears both the delayed copy and the pulse.

Real designs constantly need to turn a level into an event. Interrupt controllers raise a one cycle pulse when a peripheral flag goes high, UART receivers kick off bit sampling on the start bit edge, and DMA engines launch a transfer on a trigger line. A level that stays high for ten cycles must still produce exactly one action, and that is what this block guarantees. The input here is already synchronized, which matters: in a real design a raw pin would go through a synchronizer first, because edge detecting an unsynchronized signal risks metastability. Here we skip that stage and go straight to the detector: keep one flop of history and pulse when the input is high but its history is still low.
problems.solution:
logic d;
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (!rst_n) begin d <= 1'b0; pulse <= 1'b0; end
  else begin d <= sig; pulse <= sig && !d; end
end
problems.details:
The design keeps a delayed copy d of the input sig, updated every clock. The pulse output is combinational in spirit: pulse = sig && !d. Walk through it: when sig rises, d still holds the old 0 for exactly one cycle, so the AND is true for that one cycle. On the next edge d catches up to 1 and the AND goes false, even if sig stays high for a hundred cycles. The pulse width is exactly one clock period by construction, never a function of how long sig stays high.

Reset clears both d and pulse. Clearing d is the part people forget, and it matters: if d came out of reset holding a stale 1 while sig was 0, the first real rising edge would find d already high and produce no pulse. A missed edge out of reset is exactly the kind of bug that only shows up on the bench, so both registers get a known starting state.

This is sometimes called a poor man's one shot. The two flop structure is also the skeleton of debouncers and synchronizer chains, where the same delay and compare idea gets reused.
problems.example:
sig:   0 0 1 1 0
d:     0 0 0 1 1
pulse: 0 0 1 0 0   (exactly one cycle)

sig:   0 1 0 1 1 1 -> pulse: 0 1 0 1 0 0 (a lone high cycle still makes one pulse; a long high level makes only one)
sig held high for 5 cycles -> still exactly one pulse, on the first cycle

Failing case: reset clears pulse but the designer forgets d, and d powers up as 1 with sig at 0. The first real rising edge arrives: sig is 1, d is already 1, so pulse = 1 && !1 = 0. The edge is missed silently. Clearing both registers on reset is what prevents this.
constraints: Input is already synchronous: one flop of delay suffices.
Pulse is exactly one cycle wide.
Reset clears both d and pulse.
Falling edges produce no pulse.

quiz.q: Why is pulse <= sig && !d high for exactly one cycle?
choices: d catches up one cycle later, so the condition is true only in the first cycle sig is high
The clock stops after one cycle
quiz.why: d is sig delayed by one flop. In the first cycle sig is high, d is still low, so the AND is true. Next cycle d has caught up and the AND goes false.

quiz.q: Why does reset clear d as well as pulse?
choices: A stale value in d could suppress a real edge or fake one
d is not a real signal
Reset must clear every signal in the file
quiz.why: If d came out of reset holding a 1 while sig was 0, the first real rising edge would be missed. Clearing both gives a known starting state.

quiz.q: In a real design the input comes from an external pin. What should happen before this edge detector?
choices: The pin should pass through a synchronizer into this clock domain
The pin can feed the detector directly, no staging needed
The detector needs a faster clock than the pin
The pin must be inverted first
quiz.why: An asynchronous pin can violate the flop setup and hold times and go metastable. A synchronizer first is the standard protection; this problem skips it only because the input is specified as already synchronized.

hints: I need to know what sig was one cycle ago. A single flop holding the previous value of sig gives me that history.
The pulse is high when sig is high now but was low a cycle ago: pulse = sig && !d, with d updated to sig every clock.
Reset has to clear both d and pulse. A stale 1 in d after reset would eat the first real edge.
problems.takeaway: An edge is the input AND NOT its one cycle delayed copy, and the delay flop must reset to a known state or the first edge after reset gets missed.

problems.title: Up down counter
problems.statement:
Build an 8 bit counter with an enable and an up/down select. It counts up when up is 1 and down when up is 0, only while enable is high, and resets to zero. Also generate a terminal count output that is high when the counter is at all ones while counting up with enable.

Counters are the time base of digital design. A baud rate generator is a counter that reloads every time it hits its terminal value, and that reload tick is the bit clock. Timer peripherals raise interrupts off terminal count, FIFO fill level logic is an up/down counter tracking pushes minus pops, and link layers count retries. The terminal count output is the interesting part of this problem: it is the combinational "we are at the top" flag that downstream logic uses as its trigger, and qualifying it with up and enable is what keeps it from firing at the wrong time. Get tc wrong and a baud generator reloads early or a timer interrupts spuriously.
problems.details:
The counter is one always_ff block. On reset it goes to zero. Otherwise, when enable is high it adds or subtracts one based on up; when enable is low it simply holds, which falls out naturally from only assigning count inside the enable branch. Counting is plain unsigned arithmetic, so it wraps: counting up past 8'hFF lands on 8'h00, and counting down past 8'h00 lands on 8'hFF. That wraparound is inherent to the bit width, not something you have to code specially.

The terminal count tc is combinational: tc = (count == 8'hFF) && up && en. All three terms matter. The count comparison says we are at the top of the range, up says we are moving toward the top rather than away from it, and en says the counter is actually running. Drop any of the qualifiers and tc can fire while the counter is sitting idle at 8'hFF or while counting down through it, which is exactly how spurious reloads happen in real timer blocks.
problems.example:
count=8'hFE, en=1, up=1 -> next 8'hFF, tc=0
count=8'hFF, en=1, up=1 -> next 8'h00 (wraps), tc=1 this cycle
count=8'h05, en=0, up=1 -> stays 8'h05, tc=0
count=8'h00, en=1, up=0 -> next 8'hFF (wraps down), tc=0 (down, not up)

Failing case: tc coded as just (count == 8'hFF) with no up or en qualifiers. The counter sits at 8'hFF with en low after a burst, and tc stays asserted the whole idle period, so the baud generator it feeds keeps reloading and the bit clock never stops. Qualifying tc with up and en is what makes it a true terminal event rather than a level.
constraints: 8 bit counter, enable gated.
up=1 counts up, up=0 counts down.
Reset to zero.
tc is high only at 8'hFF with up and en high.

quiz.q: When is tc high?
choices: count is 8'hFF and up and en are both high
quiz.why: tc = (count == 8'hFF) && up && en. All three must be true: at the top of the range, counting up, and enabled.

quiz.q: With en=0, what does the counter do?
quiz.why: The else if (en) guard means the count register only updates when enable is high. With en low it keeps its value.

quiz.q: count=8'h00, en=1, up=0. What is the next count?
quiz.why: The counter is plain unsigned 8 bit arithmetic. Subtracting 1 from 0 borrows through every bit and wraps to all ones.

hints: The counter body is one always_ff: reset to zero first, then an enable branch that adds or subtracts 1 based on up.
When en is low, just do not assign count. A clocked register with no assignment keeps its value, which is the hold behavior.
tc is a separate combinational assign: high when count is all ones AND up is 1 AND en is 1. All three conditions, not just the count.
problems.takeaway: Terminal count is a qualified event, not just a value compare: the count, the direction, and the enable all have to agree or it fires at the wrong time.

problems.title: Synchronous FIFO
problems.statement:
Design a synchronous FIFO: depth 16, 8 bit data, with full, empty, and almost full flags. The tricky part is telling full apart from empty when the read and write pointers are equal. Think about what extra state resolves the ambiguity before you code it.

FIFOs are the shock absorbers of real designs. A UART TX FIFO holds bytes while the shifter drains them one bit at a time, DMA engines stage descriptors in a FIFO between the fetch and execute sides, and AXI bridges use FIFOs to absorb bursts when the downstream stalls. The full and empty flags are the handshake contract with the producer and consumer: write when not full, read when not empty. Get the flags wrong and you either drop data by writing into a full FIFO or read garbage from an empty one. Almost full exists so the producer gets one cycle of warning before the door shuts. This problem is really about the pointer comparison at the heart of every FIFO, sync or async.
problems.starter:
module fifo_sync #(
  parameter int DEPTH = 16,
  parameter int WIDTH = 8
) (
  input  logic             clk,
  input  logic             rst_n,
  input  logic             push,
  input  logic             pop,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] data_in,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] data_out,
  output logic             full,
  output logic             empty,
  output logic             almost_full
);
  // TODO: memory, read/write pointers, flag logic
endmodule
problems.solution: Reference approach: read/write pointers with extra MSB for full vs empty disambiguation.
problems.details:
Depth 16 needs a 4 bit index to address the memory, plus one extra MSB on each pointer, making 5 bit pointers. The extra bit toggles every time its pointer wraps past the end of the memory. Now the two ambiguous cases separate cleanly: empty is wr_ptr == rd_ptr with all 5 bits equal, and full is wr_ptr == rd_ptr on the lower 4 bits with the MSBs different, meaning the write pointer has lapped the read pointer exactly once.

Almost full asserts when 15 entries are stored, giving the producer one entry of warning before full. Entry count can be derived from the pointer difference, or tracked with a small counter; either way it is the same information the flags carry.

Writes are guarded by !full and reads by !empty. A simultaneous read and write is legal: both pointers advance, the entry count does not change, and the flags stay consistent. On reset both pointers clear to zero, which reads as empty, the only sane starting state. Everything here is one clock domain, which is what makes this the synchronous version; the async FIFO later in this track solves the same pointer problem across two clocks.
problems.example:
wr_ptr=5'b1_0000, rd_ptr=5'b0_0000 -> full (same index, MSB differs)
wr_ptr=5'b0_0101, rd_ptr=5'b0_0101 -> empty (fully equal)
15 entries stored -> almost_full high, full low
simultaneous push and pop with 1 entry stored -> still 1 entry, both pointers advance, empty stays low

Failing case: a designer compares plain 4 bit pointers and defines full as (wr_ptr == rd_ptr). Right after reset both pointers are 0 and the FIFO is empty, but the flag reads full, so the producer never writes a single byte and the design deadlocks on its first transaction. The extra MSB is what separates the two meanings of equal pointers.
constraints: Single clock for read and write.
Depth 16, data width 8.
