Flags: full, empty, almost full.
Full vs empty disambiguation is the core design decision.

quiz.q: Why do the pointers need an extra MSB?
choices: Equal pointers are ambiguous between full and empty; the extra bit resolves it
It is required by the AXI spec
quiz.why: With plain binary pointers, wr_ptr == rd_ptr happens both when the FIFO is empty and when it is full. The extra MSB toggles on wrap, so full and empty become distinguishable.

quiz.q: With the extra MSB scheme, what does 'full' look like?
choices: Pointer indices equal but MSBs different
quiz.why: The write pointer has lapped the read pointer exactly once: same index, MSB flipped. Fully equal pointers mean empty.

quiz.q: A push and a pop happen in the same cycle while 3 entries are stored. What is the entry count after the cycle?
choices: Still 3, both pointers advanced and the count is unchanged
4, the push wins over the pop
2, the pop wins over the push
quiz.why: One entry entered and one left in the same cycle. Both pointers move forward one slot and the net occupancy does not change.

hints: The memory is 16 deep, so the index is 4 bits. The trick is the 5th bit: add one extra MSB to each pointer that flips every time the pointer wraps.
Define the flags from the pointers: empty when the full 5 bit pointers match, full when the 4 bit indices match but the MSBs differ.
Guard the memory writes with !full and the reads with !empty, and let a simultaneous read and write advance both pointers. Almost full is the 15 entry mark.
problems.takeaway: Equal FIFO pointers mean two different things, and one extra wrap bit on each pointer is the standard way to tell full from empty.

problems.title: Sequence detector 1011
problems.statement:
Build a Mealy FSM that detects the sequence 1011 on a serial input, with overlapping sequences allowed. A found output pulses when the last bit of the pattern arrives. After a detection, the machine must stay positioned to catch a pattern that overlaps the tail of the one just found.

Pattern detectors watch serial streams in real hardware. A UART receiver hunts for the start bit edge in the incoming bit stream, link training logic looks for ordered sets on a serial lane, and protocol monitors flag magic numbers as bytes flow past. The streams never pause politely between patterns, so a detector that goes blind after each match will miss real events. That is why overlap handling is the heart of this problem: the trailing 1 of one 1011 can be the leading 1 of the next, and the state machine has to be sitting in the right state to catch it. Mealy versus Moore is the secondary lesson: the found pulse comes out in the same cycle the final bit arrives, which is what lets downstream logic react without a one cycle delay.
problems.solution: Reference approach: states S0 idle, S1 got 1, S2 got 10, S3 got 101; on 1 in S3 assert found and go to S1 for overlap.
problems.details:
Four states track the longest prefix of 1011 matched so far: idle for nothing useful, s1 for having seen a trailing 1, s10 for a trailing 10, s101 for a trailing 101. The found output is Mealy: it asserts when the state is s101 and the current input din is 1, in the same cycle the final bit of the pattern arrives. A Moore version would need a fifth state and would report the detection a cycle later.

The overlap logic lives in the transitions. From s101 on a 1, the pattern completes and the machine goes to s1, because that final 1 doubles as the first bit of a possible new pattern. From s101 on a 0, the stream ends in 1010, whose longest prefix of 1011 is 10, so the machine goes to s10 rather than all the way back to idle. That fallback behavior, always landing on the longest usable prefix, is the part most hand written detectors get wrong, and it is exactly what keeps overlapping patterns detectable.

Reset returns the machine to idle. The state register is one always_ff block; the next state and output logic are combinational, the standard two or three always block FSM split.
problems.example:
din: 1 0 1 1         -> found pulses on the 4th bit
din: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1   -> found pulses on the 4th bit and again on the 7th bit (overlap through the shared 1)
din: 1 0 0 1 1       -> no detection, pattern broken at the third bit
din: 1 1 0 1 1       -> found pulses on the 5th bit (the doubled 1 just restarts the prefix)

Failing case: after a detection the designer sends the machine back to idle instead of s1. On the stream 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 the first pattern is found at bit 4, but the second pattern, bits 4 through 7, is missed, because the machine was in idle when bit 5 arrived instead of already holding the bit 4 head start in s1. Only one pulse instead of two.
constraints: Mealy output: found depends on state and current input.
Overlapping patterns must be caught.
Reset returns to idle.
One cycle pulse per detection.

quiz.q: After detecting 1011, why go to the 'seen 1' state instead of idle?
choices: The final 1 can start a new overlapping pattern
Idle is not a real state
Mealy machines cannot go to idle
quiz.why: In the stream 10111, the last 1 of the first pattern is the first 1 of a potential second pattern. Returning to 'seen 1' keeps that overlap detectable.

quiz.q: What makes this a Mealy machine rather than a Moore machine?
choices: found depends on the current input as well as the state
quiz.why: found asserts when the machine is in the 'seen 101' state AND din is 1 right now. An output that depends on the current input is the definition of Mealy.

quiz.q: From the 'seen 101' state the input is 0, so the stream ends in 1010. Where should the machine go?
choices: 'seen 10', the longest prefix of 1011 that is a suffix of 1010
'seen 1', the last bit was 0 so start over from the 1
'seen 101', stay and wait for the next bit
quiz.why: The fallback rule is longest prefix of the pattern that matches a suffix of what was just seen. Suffixes of 1010 that are also prefixes of 1011 give 10, so the machine keeps two bits of progress instead of throwing it away.

hints: Four states are enough: idle, seen 1, seen 10, seen 101. Each state remembers the longest prefix of 1011 matched so far.
found is a Mealy output: assert it when the state is seen 101 and din is 1 right now, in the same cycle.
On every transition ask: what is the longest prefix of 1011 that is a suffix of everything seen so far? That rule gives you the overlap behavior, including going to seen 1 after a detection.
problems.takeaway: A sequence detector never throws progress away: every transition lands on the longest pattern prefix that still matches, which is what makes overlaps detectable.

problems.title: Parameterized adder
problems.statement:
Write an N bit adder with carry in, carry out, sum, and an overflow flag for the signed interpretation. The overflow logic is the part to think about: it is not the same as carry out.

Adders are the working core of every ALU, and the parameterized form is how real RTL stays reusable: one module, instantiated at 8, 16, 32, or 64 bits wherever the datapath needs it. Carry out and overflow serve two different customers. Unsigned multiword arithmetic chains adders through carry out, that is how a 128 bit sum gets built from 32 bit adders. Signed arithmetic watches the overflow flag instead: DSP filter accumulators, address offset math, and anything doing two's complement needs to know when the true result stopped fitting. The classic bug this problem vaccinates against is using carry out as the signed overflow check. For 127 + 1 in 8 bits there is no carry out, yet the signed result wrapped from +127 to -128, and code that trusted cout would sail past the error.
problems.solution: Reference approach: {cout, sum} = a + b + cin; overflow = (a[N-1] == b[N-1]) && (sum[N-1] != a[N-1]).
problems.details:
The sum and carry out come from one expression: {cout, sum} = a + b + cin. The concatenation on the left gives the addition N+1 bits of room, so the carry out of bit N-1 lands in cout instead of being silently dropped. Carry in folds into the same expression, and it is what makes subtraction free: a - b is just a + ~b + 1, addition with the subtrahend inverted and cin set.

Overflow is purely about the signed interpretation. In two's complement, adding two numbers of the same sign can never legitimately change the sign, so overflow is exactly the condition (a[N-1] == b[N-1]) && (sum[N-1] != a[N-1]): same sign in, different sign out. An equivalent formulation XORs the carry into the top bit with the carry out of it. Note that cin participates in the sum but the textbook overflow expression above already accounts for it through sum[N-1], so no special casing is needed.

Everything here is combinational: one continuous assignment for the sum and carry, one for overflow. No clock, no state.
problems.example:
N=8: a=8'h7F, b=8'h01, cin=0 -> sum=8'h80, cout=0, overflow=1 (+127 + 1 wrapped to -128)
N=8: a=8'hFF, b=8'h01, cin=0 -> sum=8'h00, cout=1, overflow=0 (-1 + 1 = 0, clean)
N=8: a=8'h80, b=8'hFF, cin=0 -> sum=8'h7F, cout=1, overflow=1 (-128 + -1 wrapped to +127)
N=8: a=8'h0A, b=8'h05, cin=1 -> sum=8'h10, cout=0, overflow=0 (10 + 5 + 1 = 16)

Failing case: the designer reports cout as the signed overflow flag. For a=8'h7F, b=8'h01 the carry out is 0, so their check says no overflow, while the signed result actually wrapped from +127 to -128. Carry out answers the unsigned question; the sign bit comparison answers the signed one.
constraints: Parameterized width N, default 8.
Ports: a, b, cin, sum, cout, overflow.
overflow is for the signed interpretation.
carry out and overflow are different signals.

quiz.q: In the example a=8'h7F + 8'h01, why is overflow 1 while cout is 0?
choices: Two positive signed inputs produced a negative result: signed overflow, with no unsigned carry
quiz.why: 0x7F is +127 and 0x01 is +1 in signed 8 bit; the true sum +128 does not fit, and the result 0x80 reads as -128. Same sign in, different sign out means signed overflow. Unsigned, 127+1=128 produces no carry out of bit 7, so cout is 0.

quiz.q: What does (a[N-1] == b[N-1]) && (sum[N-1] != a[N-1]) detect?
choices: Signed overflow: same sign inputs, different sign result
quiz.why: It is true exactly when both inputs share a sign bit and the sum's sign bit differs: the textbook condition for two's complement overflow.

quiz.q: How do you compute a - b using this adder?
choices: a + ~b + 1: invert b and set cin to 1
a + b with cin set to 1
quiz.why: Two's complement negation is invert and add one. Folding the plus one into cin gives subtraction from the same adder hardware.

hints: One expression gives you sum and carry out together: {cout, sum} = a + b + cin. The concatenation makes room for the carry.
Overflow is not the carry out. Think about signs: when can adding two same sign numbers legitimately flip the sign bit?
overflow = (a[N-1] == b[N-1]) && (sum[N-1] != a[N-1]). Same sign going in, different sign coming out.
problems.takeaway: Carry out belongs to unsigned arithmetic and the sign bit comparison belongs to signed arithmetic, and confusing the two is how 127 + 1 silently becomes -128.

problems.title: Binary to gray converter
problems.statement:
Convert an N bit binary value to Gray code with a parameterized module. There is a one line combinational expression for this. Think about what each Gray bit is in terms of the binary bits.

Gray code earns its keep wherever a counter crosses into another clock domain. Async FIFO read and write pointers travel between clocks in Gray code, because consecutive values differ in exactly one bit: if the synchronizer samples the pointer mid transition, the worst it can see is one of the two adjacent values, never a garbage word. The same property is why rotary encoders output Gray code; a mechanical contact bouncing between positions cannot produce a wildly wrong reading. This problem builds the encoder half of that story: binary in, Gray out, one line of combinational logic.
problems.solution: Reference approach: gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1).
problems.details:
Each Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits: gray[i] = bin[i+1] ^ bin[i] for the lower bits, and the MSB passes through unchanged, gray[N-1] = bin[N-1]. The whole conversion collapses into one expression: gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1). Shifting right by one lines up bin[i+1] with position i, and the XOR does all the adjacent pair folds at once. The shift drops in a 0 at the top, so the MSB XORs with 0 and passes through, exactly matching the per bit definition.

The module is parameterized on N and purely combinational. One direction is worth knowing for later: converting Gray back to binary is a prefix XOR chain, where each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits above it. You will need that direction when you compare synchronized Gray pointers in the async FIFO problem.
problems.example:
bin=4'b0001 -> gray=4'b0001
bin=4'b0010 -> gray=4'b0011
bin=4'b0100 -> gray=4'b0110
bin=4'b0111 -> gray=4'b0100 (7 to 8 in binary is 0111 to 1000, four bits flip; in Gray it is 0100 to 1100, one bit flips)
bin=4'b1111 -> gray=4'b1000 (edge case at the top of the range)

Failing case: a designer writes gray = bin ^ (bin << 1), shifting the wrong way. For bin=4'b0010 this gives 4'b0110 instead of the correct 4'b0011, and the single bit change property is destroyed. The shift has to go right so that each Gray bit folds bit i+1 down onto bit i.
constraints: Parameterized width N, default 8.
Purely combinational, one line.
MSB of gray equals MSB of bin.
Consecutive values differ in one bit.

quiz.q: In gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1), what is gray[N-1]?
choices: Equal to bin[N-1], since the shifted value has 0 at the top
quiz.why: bin >> 1 shifts a 0 into the MSB position, so gray[N-1] = bin[N-1] ^ 0 = bin[N-1]. The top bit passes through.

quiz.q: Why is Gray code used for FIFO pointers crossing clock domains?
choices: Consecutive values differ in one bit, so a sampled pointer is at most one count off
quiz.why: Only one bit changes per count, so even if the synchronizer samples mid transition, the result is one of the two adjacent values: never a wildly wrong pointer.

quiz.q: Binary 7 is 0111 and binary 8 is 1000. What changes between Gray(7) and Gray(8)?
choices: No bits, they share a code
quiz.why: That is the whole point of Gray code: consecutive values always differ in a single bit, even across the 0111 to 1000 boundary where binary flips every bit.

hints: Each Gray bit is the XOR of two neighboring binary bits: gray[i] = bin[i+1] ^ bin[i], with the top bit passing through.
You can do all of those folds at once. Shifting bin right by one lines up each bin[i+1] with position i.
The one liner is: gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1). Check the MSB: the shift puts a 0 there, so the top bit survives unchanged.
problems.takeaway: Gray code is one XOR away from binary, and its single bit change property is what makes counters safe to sample across clock domains.

problems.title: Asynchronous FIFO
problems.statement:
Design a dual clock FIFO with Gray coded pointers, two flop synchronizers, and full/empty generation in the respective clock domains. The core problem is comparing pointers that live in different clock domains without metastability corrupting the comparison.

This is the block that moves data between unrelated clocks, and unrelated clocks are everywhere: a UART receiver running on its own baud derived clock feeding a CPU bus, an ADC streaming samples into a DSP domain, SerDes lanes handing packets to core logic. It is also the standard interview probe for whether someone truly understands clock domain crossing, because every design decision in it has a reason. The architecture: each side keeps its pointer in binary, converts to Gray before crossing, pushes it through a two flop synchronizer into the other domain, and generates full in the write domain and empty in the read domain. The flags come out conservative by construction: full can assert a touch early and empty can assert a touch early, but neither ever asserts late, which is exactly the safe direction.
problems.starter:
module fifo_async #(
  parameter int DEPTH = 16,
  parameter int WIDTH = 8
) (
  input  logic             wr_clk,
  input  logic             rd_clk,
  input  logic             wr_rst_n,
  input  logic             rd_rst_n,
  input  logic             push,
  input  logic             pop,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] data_in,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] data_out,
  output logic             full,
  output logic             empty
);
  // TODO: gray pointers, synchronizers, full/empty per domain
endmodule
problems.solution: Reference approach: convert binary pointers to gray before crossing, synchronize with two flops each way, compare synchronized gray pointers for full and empty.
problems.details:
Start from the synchronous FIFO pointer trick and add the crossing problem. Binary pointers cannot cross directly: a count like 0111 to 1000 flips four bits at once, and a synchronizer sampling mid transition can resolve to any of the intermediate bit patterns, a garbage pointer that corrupts the full and empty comparison. Gray code fixes this because only one bit changes per count, so the worst case sample is one of the two adjacent values, off by at most one entry.

Each pointer crosses in Gray form through two back to back flops in the receiving domain. The two flops give a first flop that may go metastable a full clock period to settle before the second flop samples it. Full is generated in the write domain by comparing the local write Gray pointer against the synchronized read Gray pointer; empty is generated symmetrically in the read domain. The domain that acts on a flag generates it: the write side decides whether to accept a push, so full must be synchronous to wr_clk, and likewise empty to rd_clk.

Because the synchronized pointer always lags the real one, the comparisons err on the safe side. Full may assert when one slot is still free, which only stops writes a cycle early. Empty may assert when data has actually arrived, which only makes the read side wait a cycle. A flag that is early is a minor throughput cost; a flag that is late is data corruption, so conservative is the correct engineering call.

The full comparison on Gray pointers has a specific form for a depth 2^N FIFO: full when the write Gray pointer equals the synchronized read Gray pointer with the top two bits inverted and the rest equal, which is the Gray encoding of the write pointer having lapped the read pointer exactly once. Empty is the simple case: the two Gray pointers fully equal.
problems.example:
wr_ptr_gray crosses to rd domain -> empty is computed there from the synchronized copy
rd_ptr_gray crosses to wr domain -> full is computed there from the synchronized copy
full may assert early by one entry: safe and conservative, never late
empty may assert early by one entry: the read side waits a cycle, no garbage is read

Failing case: a designer crosses the binary pointers directly through the synchronizers to save the Gray converters. When wr_ptr counts 4'b0111 to 4'b1000, four bits flip at once, and the read domain samples 4'b0000 mid transition. The empty logic now believes the FIFO is empty when it holds 8 entries, the consumer stalls, and the producer eventually blocks on a full flag computed from equally garbage data. The deadlock only appears under specific timing, which is why this bug survives simulation and dies on the bench.
constraints: Two independent clocks and resets.
Gray code pointers for crossing.
Two flop synchronizer each direction.
full generated in write domain, empty in read domain.

quiz.q: Why must pointers cross in Gray code rather than binary?
choices: Binary pointers can change many bits at once, which a synchronizer can sample as a garbage value
quiz.why: A binary count like 0111 to 1000 flips 4 bits. If the synchronizer catches the transition mid flight, the sampled value can be anything. Gray changes one bit per count, so the worst case sample is off by one.

quiz.q: Why is full generated in the write clock domain?
choices: The write side owns push, so it must know authoritatively when to stop
The read side has no clock
Full is a Gray code signal
quiz.why: The domain that acts on a flag should generate it from its own clock. The write logic decides whether to accept a push, so full must be synchronous to wr_clk.

quiz.q: The synchronized read pointer lags the real one by a couple of write clocks. What does that imply for the full flag?
choices: Full can assert early but never late, which is the safe direction
Full can assert late, dropping data
The lag has no effect on correctness
Empty is generated in the write domain instead
quiz.why: A lagging read pointer makes the FIFO look fuller than it is. Stopping writes a cycle early costs a little throughput; letting a write through into a truly full FIFO corrupts data.

hints: Never compare a pointer against a value from the other domain directly. Convert each binary pointer to Gray, then push it through two flops in the receiving clock domain.

Generate each flag where it is used: full in the write domain from the write pointer and the synchronized read pointer, empty in the read domain from the read pointer and the synchronized write pointer.
Remember the flags are conservative by design. A synchronized pointer that lags makes full assert early, which only costs throughput, never correctness.
problems.takeaway: Cross pointers in Gray code through two flops, generate each flag in the domain that acts on it, and let the flags err early rather than late.

problems.title: Pipelined multiplier
problems.statement:
Build an 8x8 multiplier with 3 pipeline stages. A valid signal must travel through the pipeline alongside the data so the consumer knows when the product is real, and reset must flush every stage.

A single cycle 8x8 multiply is easy to write and easy to time at low clock speeds, but the combinational path through the partial products and the adder tree grows fast and becomes the critical path as frequency climbs. Pipelining is the standard trade: accept 3 cycles of latency in exchange for one result per clock, which is throughput the single cycle version cannot touch at speed. This is how real multiply accumulate units are built, from DSP blocks in FPGAs to the MAC arrays in AI accelerators. The valid bit is the part beginners drop: a pipeline always contains something, including garbage after reset and bubbles between real inputs, so the data means nothing without a marker saying which emerging product corresponds to a real input pair.
problems.starter:
module pipe_mult (
  input  logic        clk,
  input  logic        rst_n,
  input  logic        valid_in,
  input  logic [7:0]  a,
  input  logic [7:0]  b,
  output logic        valid_out,
  output logic [15:0] product
);
  // TODO: 3 pipeline stages, valid shift register, reset flush
endmodule
problems.solution: Reference approach: register operands in stage 1, partial products in stage 2, final sum in stage 3; shift a valid bit through the same stages; clear all stages on reset.
problems.details:
The data path registers operands in stage 1, partial products in stage 2, and the final sum in stage 3, so a product fed in at cycle 0 emerges at cycle 3. A separate 3 bit shift register carries the valid bit through identical staging: valid_in sampled at cycle 0 becomes valid_out at cycle 3, aligned exactly with its product. The consumer qualifies every read of the product with valid_out and ignores anything else coming out of the pipe.

Reset must flush every stage, data and valid alike. After a reset the pipeline holds stale operands from before the reset, and without a flush those would march out over the next three cycles looking like fresh results. Clearing the data stages and the valid shift register together guarantees the first valid_out after reset corresponds to the first real input pair after reset, with no phantom products in between.

Throughput after the pipe fills is one product per clock; latency is a fixed 3 cycles. That fixed latency is what makes the traveling valid bit a simple shift register rather than a counter or a FIFO.
problems.example:
valid_in=1 at c0 -> valid_out=1 at c3 with the product of c0's operands
valid_in=0 at c1 -> valid_out=0 at c4, product ignored (a bubble in the pipe)
reset at c2 -> all stages cleared, valid_out=0 at c5
back to back valid inputs at c0, c1, c2 -> valid products emerge at c3, c4, c5, one per clock

Failing case: the designer pipelines the data through 3 stages but delays valid by only 1 flop. With valid_in=1 at c0, valid_out fires at c1 while the real product is still two stages deep in the pipe, so the consumer latches whatever stale value sits at the output and treats it as the answer. The valid delay must equal the data latency exactly, stage for stage.
constraints: 8 bit inputs, 16 bit product.
Exactly 3 pipeline stages.
valid travels in lockstep with data.
Reset flushes every stage.

quiz.q: Why does the valid signal need its own shift register?
choices: To mark which pipeline slot holds a real result, aligned with the data
Valid signals cannot go through flops
quiz.why: The pipeline always contains something, including garbage after reset or bubbles. The traveling valid bit says which emerging product corresponds to a real input pair.

quiz.q: What does 'reset must flush every stage' prevent?
choices: Stale partial results emerging as valid products after reset
quiz.why: Without a flush, old operands sitting in the pipeline would emerge after reset looking like fresh results. Clearing all stages, including the valid shift register, prevents that.

quiz.q: After the pipeline fills, what are the throughput and latency?
choices: One product per clock, 3 cycles of latency
One product every 3 clocks, 1 cycle of latency
Three products per clock, 3 cycles of latency
One product per clock, 1 cycle of latency
quiz.why: Each stage hands its result forward every clock, so a finished product emerges every cycle once the pipe is full. Any single input still takes 3 cycles to travel end to end.

hints: Split the multiply into 3 register stages: operands, partial products, final sum. Every stage boundary gets a flop.
valid_in needs the same treatment as the data: a 3 flop shift register so valid_out lines up with the product it belongs to.
On reset, clear all three data stages AND the valid shift register. Otherwise stale operands walk out after reset looking like real results.
problems.takeaway: A pipeline is only as correct as its valid bit: delay the marker by exactly the data latency and flush every stage on reset.

problems.title: Round robin arbiter
problems.statement:
Design a 4 client round robin arbiter with rotating priority. The grant must hold until the winning request drops. Think about where the priority pointer lives and exactly when it advances.

Arbiters guard every shared resource in a real SoC. An AXI interconnect arbitrates masters onto a shared slave port, a memory controller arbitrates requestors onto the DRAM command bus, and NoC routers arbitrate packets onto output ports. Fixed priority is simpler to write but it starves the low priority clients whenever a high priority one is busy, and starvation in a memory controller is a system hang with extra steps. Round robin fixes that by rotating priority: whoever was served last goes to the back of the line. Two behaviors define correctness here and both are about timing: the grant must hold steady until the winner's request drops, and the priority pointer must advance past the grantee exactly when that happens, not before and not every cycle.
problems.solution: Reference approach: keep a rotating priority pointer, grant the highest priority active requester at or after the pointer, advance the pointer past the grantee when its request drops.
problems.details:
A priority pointer, a 2 bit register for 4 clients, remembers where the next arbitration search starts. The grant logic scans requests at and after the pointer, wrapping around to the low clients if needed, and issues a one hot grant to the first active requester found. Masking the requests below the pointer and ORing in a wrapped search is the standard implementation, and it keeps the logic shallow.

The grant holds until the winning request drops. No re arbitration mid transfer: if the arbiter re evaluated every cycle, a newly arrived higher priority request could steal the grant halfway through a burst and corrupt it. Holding is what turns the grant into a transfer sized commitment instead of a cycle by cycle suggestion.

The pointer advances past the grantee when its request drops, which is the moment the grant ends. Advancing on grant issue instead would rotate priority while the winner still holds the bus, and advancing every cycle would chatter the grant. After the pointer moves, the next arbitration starts from the following client, which is what delivers the fairness: back to back requests from all four clients get served in rotation with no starvation. On reset the pointer goes to 0 and the grant clears.
problems.example:
pointer=0, req=4'b1010 -> gnt=4'b0010 (client 1, first at/after pointer)
client 1 drops req -> pointer advances to 2
pointer=2, req=4'b1001 -> gnt=4'b1000 (client 3, wrap search past client 0)
req=4'b0000 -> gnt=4'b0000, pointer holds (no requester, nothing to do)
req=4'b1111 held for 4 transfers -> grants rotate 0,1,2,3 in order, no starvation

Failing case: the pointer advances when the grant is issued rather than when the request drops. Client 1 wins the grant and holds its request for a 4 beat burst, but the pointer has already moved on, so when client 2 raises its request mid burst the arbiter re assigns the grant to client 2. Client 1's transfer is cut in half and the peripheral sees a corrupted burst. Advancing on drop instead of on grant is what keeps the winner whole.
constraints: 4 clients.
Rotating priority, not fixed.
Grant holds until the winner's request drops.
Pointer advances past the grantee on drop.

quiz.q: When does the priority pointer advance?
choices: When the granted client's request drops
quiz.why: The pointer marks where the next search starts. It moves past the grantee only after that grant is done, i.e. when its request drops.

quiz.q: Why must the grant hold until the request drops?
choices: Re arbitrating mid transfer could yank the grant away from an unfinished transfer
Clients require a one cycle grant
quiz.why: If the arbiter re evaluated every cycle, a higher priority request arriving mid transfer would steal the grant. Holding guarantees the winner keeps the bus until it is done.

quiz.q: Why round robin instead of fixed priority?
choices: Fixed priority can starve low priority clients under continuous high priority load
Fixed priority cannot grant to more than one client
quiz.why: With fixed priority, a busy high priority requester blocks everyone below it forever. Rotating the priority gives every requester a turn, which is the fairness guarantee.

hints: Keep a 2 bit priority pointer. The grant goes to the first active requester at or after the pointer, wrapping around to the low clients.
The grant must not change while the winner still wants the bus: hold it until that client's request drops.
Advance the pointer past the grantee at the moment its request drops, not when the grant is issued and not every cycle.
problems.takeaway: Round robin fairness lives in the pointer timing: hold the grant for the whole transfer and rotate priority exactly when the winner lets go.

problems.title: CDC synchronizer plus SVA
problems.statement:
Write a two flop synchronizer for a single bit crossing clock domains, plus assertions that check the synchronizer is built right: no combinational logic between the two flops, and the synchronized output is only used after the full 2 cycle latency.

Single control bits cross clock domains constantly: an interrupt line into a CPU clock domain, a data ready flag from a sensor domain, a reset release fanning out to another clock. The two flop synchronizer is the standard answer for one bit, and the reason is settling time: the first flop can go metastable when the input changes too close to the destination clock edge, and the second flop samples it a full cycle later, giving it maximum time to resolve to a clean 0 or 1 before anything uses it. The assertions in this problem are structural checks, the kind of thing a CDC lint tool verifies: they prove the synchronizer was actually built as two back to back flops and that downstream logic respects the latency instead of reaching in early.
problems.solution: Reference approach: two back to back flops with nothing between them; assert that downstream logic samples the second flop output only.
problems.details:
The synchronizer is two flip flops in series in the destination clock domain, with nothing but a wire between them. That nothing is load bearing: any combinational logic between the flops would eat into the full clock period of settling time the second flop provides, directly weakening the metastability protection. Synthesis must also be told not to optimize the structure away, which in real flows is done with attributes that preserve the flops and keep them adjacent, but the structural requirement is the same either way.

The synchronized output is valid 2 destination clocks after the source changes, one cycle per flop, and downstream logic must consume only dout, never the intermediate flop. Sampling the first flop early to save a cycle of latency defeats the entire purpose: the first flop's output is the one that can be metastable.

The assertions check two properties. First, a structural one: there is no logic between flop 1 and flop 2, so the settling time is intact. Second, a protocol one: the consumer only samples dout after the full 2 cycle latency has elapsed since the source changed. Together they turn tribal knowledge about how synchronizers must be built into checks the tools enforce every run.

One honest boundary: this synchronizer is for a single bit. A multi bit bus crossing needs a FIFO or a handshake, because two flops per bit cannot keep the bits of a bus aligned with each other.
problems.example:
din toggles in src domain -> appears at dout 2 dst clocks later
assertion: no gates between flop 1 and flop 2
downstream samples dout only, never the intermediate flop
reset: both flops clear together so no stale synchronized value survives

Failing case: downstream logic samples the first flop's output directly to save one cycle of latency. That node is exactly the one that can be metastable, so the X propagates into the destination logic and the saved cycle buys a corrupted control signal. The 2 cycle latency is the price of the protection; reaching in early voids the warranty.
constraints: Single bit crossing.
Two flops, back to back, in the destination domain.
No combinational logic between the flops.
Output valid only after 2 destination clocks.

quiz.q: Why must there be no combinational logic between the two flops?
choices: The second flop needs the full clock period for the first flop's output to settle
Logic between flops is illegal syntax
It would make the design faster
quiz.why: The first flop may go metastable. The second flop samples it a full cycle later, giving it maximum time to resolve. Extra logic eats into that settling time.

quiz.q: Why does the synchronized output take 2 destination clocks to be valid?
choices: Each flop adds one cycle of latency
quiz.why: The bit passes through two sequential flops in the destination domain, one cycle each, so the earliest trustworthy value appears two dst_clk edges after the source change.

quiz.q: An 8 bit data bus needs to cross clock domains. Why is one two flop synchronizer per bit the wrong answer?
choices: The bits can settle at different times, so the bus can be sampled as a mix of old and new values
Two flop synchronizers only work on single bit inputs by law
Assertions cannot be written for buses
quiz.why: Each bit resolves independently, so the sampled word can combine some old bits with some new bits into a value that was never sent. Buses need a FIFO or handshake to stay coherent.

hints: Two flops in series in the destination domain: din feeds flop 1, flop 1 feeds flop 2, flop 2 drives dout. Nothing else between them.
The latency is 2 destination clocks, one per flop. Downstream logic may only use dout, never the node between the flops.
For the assertions, check the structure (no logic between the flops) and the protocol (dout is only consumed after the full 2 cycle latency).
problems.takeaway: A two flop synchronizer trades 2 cycles of latency for metastability protection, and any shortcut around either flop voids the trade.

problems.title: Name the components
problems.statement: A UVM testbench is built from a driver, sequencer, monitor, agent, scoreboard, env, and test. For each component, write one line: what its job is and what it talks to. This is the map everything else hangs on. I treat this as the orientation exercise for week one on any real project. When a bug report says the monitor dropped a transaction, you need to know instantly that the monitor only observes and never drives, so the fix belongs in the driver or the sequencer, not the monitor. When a test hangs, you need to know the driver waits on the sequencer, so a starved driver means no sequence was started. Every later problem, from the config db to the register model, assumes you can point at any component and say who feeds it and who it feeds.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Driver: takes sequence items from the sequencer and drives them onto the pins, cycle by cycle.
2. Sequencer: arbitrates between sequences and hands items to the driver when it asks.
3. Monitor: watches the pins passively, rebuilds transactions, and broadcasts them on analysis ports.
4. Agent: packages a sequencer, driver, and monitor for one interface; is_active switches active vs passive.
5. Scoreboard: subscribes to monitor transactions and checks actual behavior against expected.
6. Env: instantiates and connects agents, scoreboards, and coverage; the reusable unit of the testbench.
7. Test: configures the env, raises objections, starts sequences, and defines pass or fail.
problems.details: Before building anything in UVM, learn the cast. Seven components make up a standard testbench: driver, sequencer, monitor, agent, scoreboard, env, and test. Each has one job and a defined set of neighbors. The driver pulls sequence items from the sequencer through its seq_item_port and turns them into pin wiggles on the virtual interface. The sequencer arbitrates sequences and serves items to the driver through its seq_item_export. The monitor watches the pins passively, rebuilds transactions, and publishes them on analysis ports to anyone subscribed. The agent bundles the sequencer, driver, and monitor for one interface, with an is_active knob that drops the sequencer and driver in passive mode. The scoreboard subscribes to the monitor stream and decides pass or fail. The env instantiates agents and scoreboards and wires the analysis ports together. The test configures the env, applies factory overrides, and starts the default sequence. This problem asks for one line per component: what it does and what it talks to. Everything later hangs on this map.
problems.example:
driver    -> takes items from the sequencer, drives pins
sequencer -> arbitrates sequences, serves items to the driver
monitor   -> watches pins, publishes transactions on analysis ports
agent     -> bundles sequencer + driver + monitor for one interface
scoreboard-> subscribes to the monitor stream, decides pass or fail
env       -> instantiates agents and scoreboard, connects analysis ports
test      -> configures the env, starts the default sequence

WRONG variant: driver -> generates random transactions and compares them against expected. This is wrong because generation belongs to sequences running on the sequencer and comparison belongs to the scoreboard. If you mix up the jobs you will wire the wrong TLM ports and the testbench will compile but nothing will run the way you expect.
constraints: Seven components, one line each.
Each line names the job and the connections.
Order follows the data flow.
No code, just the map.

quiz.q: Which component translates sequence items into pin wiggles?
quiz.why: The driver pulls items from the sequencer via seq_item_port and drives them onto the interface pins cycle by cycle.

choices: Sequencer, driver, and monitor for one interface
The config db and the factory
quiz.q: What does the agent package together?
quiz.why: Per the key points, an agent bundles a sequencer, driver, and monitor for one interface, with is_active selecting active vs passive mode.

choices: The sequencer, because no sequence was started on it
The monitor, because it is not publishing
The scoreboard, because it is not checking
The env, because it built the driver wrong
quiz.q: Your test hangs and the driver is stuck waiting on get_next_item. Which component is starving it?
quiz.why: get_next_item blocks until the sequencer has an item to hand over. If no sequence is running on that sequencer, the driver waits forever.

hints: Think of the data path as a one way street: sequences to sequencer to driver to pins, then monitor back up to scoreboard.
Each component has exactly one producer and one consumer. Ask who hands it work and who receives its output.
The monitor never drives anything and the scoreboard never touches pins. If your line gives either of them a driving job, swap it.
problems.takeaway: Every UVM component has one job and fixed neighbors, so when something breaks you know exactly where to look by following the data path.

problems.title: Transaction class
problems.statement: Write a packet transaction class extending uvm_sequence_item. It needs a rand 8 bit addr constrained inside 0 to 255, a rand 8 bit data constrained to never be zero, and the uvm_object_utils registration macro so the factory knows about it. The transaction is the currency of a real testbench: it is the packet your AXI or APB driver will drive and your monitor will reconstruct. I always tie the constraints to the DUT spec. If the spec says a data value of zero is illegal on this interface, the constraint must forbid it, because a random zero will send you chasing a phantom DUT bug that was really your stimulus.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Extend uvm_sequence_item so the class can travel through sequencers and drivers.
2. Declare rand bit [7:0] addr and rand bit [7:0] data.
3. Constrain addr with inside {[0:255]} and data with data != 0.
4. Register with `uvm_object_utils(packet) for factory creation and field automation.
5. Add a constructor calling super.new(name), and a convert2string for debuggability.
problems.details: The transaction is the currency of a UVM testbench: everything the driver drives and the monitor observes is an object of a sequence item class. This problem builds a packet class extending uvm_sequence_item with two rand fields: an 8 bit addr constrained to 0 to 255 and an 8 bit data constrained to never be zero. The uvm_object_utils macro registers the class with the factory so type_id::create works and overrides are possible, and it enables the field automation for copy, compare, and print. The constructor takes a name string and calls super.new(name), which is the UVM convention every component and object follows. A convert2string method gives you readable debug output when a transaction prints in a message.
constraints: Extends uvm_sequence_item.
addr inside [0:255], data != 0.
Registered with uvm_object_utils.
Constructor calls super.new(name).

choices: So it can travel through sequencers and drivers
Plain classes cannot have rand fields
The factory requires it for compilation
quiz.q: Why must the class extend uvm_sequence_item instead of a plain class?
quiz.why: Sequencers and drivers are typed to uvm_sequence_item. Only items extending it can be passed through seq_item_port and started on sequencers.

choices: Registers the class with the factory for creation and field automation
quiz.q: What does `uvm_object_utils(packet) do?
quiz.why: The macro registers the type with the UVM factory so it can be created by type_id::create and overridden, and it enables automated copy, compare, and print.

choices: The uvm_object_utils macro is missing, so the factory never learned the type
The rand fields were not constrained
quiz.q: You call packet::type_id::create("p") and get a null handle back. What is the most likely cause?

The constraint on data is a simple inequality. The addr range fits in 8 bits, so the constraint just documents the legal space.
If create returns null, the missing piece is the macro that introduces the class to the factory.
