problems.title: Simple driver
problems.statement: Write the run phase of a driver that plays a valid/ready handshake. For each sequence item: wait until ready is high, assert valid with the item data for one cycle, then deassert. Pull items with get_next_item and release them with item_done. The driver is the one piece of a real testbench that must be cycle accurate to the protocol. Every AXI, APB, or custom streaming interface I have verified had exactly this loop at its heart. Get the handshake wrong and you will spend days staring at waveforms arguing about whether the bug is in the DUT or in your driver.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. In run_phase, loop forever: seq_item_port.get_next_item(req).
2. Wait for the interface ready with @(posedge vif.clk iff vif.ready).
3. Drive vif.valid <= 1 and vif.data <= req.data for one clock, then deassert valid.
4. Call seq_item_port.item_done() so the sequencer can hand over the next item.
5. Keep reset handling simple: drop valid whenever reset asserts.
problems.details: The driver is where transactions become waveforms. Its run phase loops forever: pull the next item with get_next_item, wait for the interface ready, assert valid with the item data for one cycle, then deassert and call item_done so the sequencer hands over the next item. get_next_item blocks the sequencer until item_done is called, which is the flow control between stimulus generation and pin driving. Reset handling stays simple: drop valid whenever reset asserts, because driving through reset is a protocol violation on most interfaces. The valid/ready handshake in the driver mirrors the protocol the DUT speaks, and the monitor on the other side reconstructs the same transactions independently.
problems.example:
get_next_item(req) -> wait ready -> valid=1, data=req.data (1 cycle)
-> valid=0 -> item_done() -> next item
reset asserts mid drive -> valid dropped immediately

WRONG variant: the driver asserts valid with the item data immediately, without waiting for ready, and never calls item_done.
This is wrong twice. Driving valid while ready is low violates the handshake the DUT expects, and skipping item_done leaves the sequencer blocked forever, so the second item never arrives and the test hangs after one transfer.
constraints: Pull items with get_next_item, release with item_done.
Wait for ready before asserting valid.
valid high for exactly one cycle per item.
Drop valid on reset.

choices: The sequencer waits forever and the test hangs
The driver skips to the next item
quiz.q: What happens if the driver never calls item_done()?
quiz.why: get_next_item blocks the sequencer until item_done is called. Forgetting it stalls the sequence and the test never finishes.

choices: Driving data while the receiver is not ready violates the handshake
It makes the test run faster
quiz.q: Why wait for ready before asserting valid?
quiz.why: In a valid/ready handshake the transfer only happens when both are high. Asserting valid while ready is low is at best wasted, at worst a protocol violation.

choices: The monitor may reconstruct a duplicate transaction and the scoreboard sees extra data
quiz.q: The driver holds valid high for two cycles per item instead of one. What breaks?
quiz.why: The monitor counts transfers, not intentions. Two valid cycles look like two transfers, so the scoreboard compares against a transaction that was never meant to exist.

hints: The loop has a fixed rhythm: get the item, wait for the handshake, drive for one cycle, release the item.
get_next_item and item_done are a matched pair. The sequencer cannot move on until you release.
Reset is the exception path: when it asserts, stop driving immediately, then go back to the top of the loop.
problems.takeaway: The driver turns items into protocol-correct waveforms: wait for ready, drive valid for exactly one cycle, release with item_done, and drop everything on reset.

problems.title: Config db
problems.statement: The virtual interface lives in the top module, but the driver needs it. Write the two calls that matter: the set in top that publishes the interface, and the get in the driver build_phase that picks it up. Get the scope strings and the parameterized types right. This is the handoff every real testbench performs in its first week of bringup. The top module owns the physical interface instance, the driver sits three levels down in the hierarchy, and the config db is the standard bridge between them. I have seen more bringup days lost to a wrong scope string or a mismatched parameterized type than to any other single cause.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. In top: uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agent.drv", "vif", vif).
2. In the driver build_phase: uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif), and `uvm_fatal if it fails.
3. The set scope string must match the driver hierarchy path; "" in get means this component level.
4. Always check the return value: a missing interface should fail loudly in build, not hang in run.
problems.details: The virtual interface is created in the top module, but the driver that needs it sits deep in the testbench hierarchy. The uvm_config_db is the bridge: top calls set with a scope string matching the driver's hierarchical path, and the driver's build_phase calls get to pick it up. The parameterized type must be the virtual interface type on both sides, and it must match exactly: virtual my_if on one side and plain my_if on the other is a different type and the get will fail. The set must happen before run_test builds the hierarchy, which is why it lives in an initial block in top. A failed get must be fatal in build: a missing interface should fail loudly, not hang in run.
problems.example:
top: uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if)::set(null,
       "uvm_test_top.env.agent.drv", "vif", vif);
driver build_phase: uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if)::get(
       this, "", "vif", vif) or `uvm_fatal

WRONG variant: top publishes with uvm_config_db#(my_if)::set (missing the virtual keyword) while the driver calls get with uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if).
This is wrong because the parameterized types do not match, so the lookup finds nothing and the get fails. The driver then fatals in build, and the error message points at the driver even though the real bug is the missing virtual keyword in top.
constraints: set in top, get in driver build_phase.
Scope string matches the driver hierarchy path.
Parameterized type is the virtual interface.
Failed get is fatal.

choices: Look up the setting at this component's own level
quiz.q: In the driver's get call, what does the empty string "" mean?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the get scope "" means this component level: it looks for a setting targeted at the driver instance itself.

choices: A missing interface would hang in run_phase; failing fast in build is louder and clearer
quiz.q: Why should a failed get be uvm_fatal in build_phase?
quiz.why: Without the interface the driver has nothing to drive. Catching it in build with a fatal stops the test immediately with a clear message instead of a mysterious hang later.

choices: The driver build already ran, so the get finds nothing and fatals
The set overwrites the interface cleanly
The driver picks it up late in run_phase
quiz.q: The set call is placed after run_test() in the top module. What happens?
quiz.why: run_test builds the whole hierarchy, so every build_phase get executes before a later set runs. Ordering matters: publish before you build.

hints: Two calls, two places: top publishes with set, the driver collects with get in build_phase.
The scope string in top must name the exact hierarchical path of the driver, and the field name must match on both sides.
The parameterized type has to be identical on both calls, virtual keyword included.
problems.takeaway: The config db hands the virtual interface from top to the driver: set before run_test with the exact scope path, get in build_phase with the identical virtual interface type, fatal on failure.

problems.title: Phases
problems.statement: List the eight main UVM phases in execution order: build_phase, connect_phase, end_of_elaboration_phase, start_of_simulation_phase, run_phase, extract_phase, check_phase, report_phase. For each one, write a single line on what belongs there. The phase order is the schedule every test on a real project runs on. I keep coming back to two facts when I debug: build runs top down so a parent cannot touch its children yet, and run is the only phase that consumes time, which is why objections live there. Most mysterious hangs I have chased turned out to be something placed in the wrong phase.
problems.starter: // TODO: the eight phases in order, one line each
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. build_phase: create components top down; read config db settings.
2. connect_phase: connect ports and exports bottom up (the TLM wiring).
3. end_of_elaboration_phase: print topology, fine tune after all connections exist.
4. start_of_simulation_phase: set drain times and final runtime knobs before time starts.
5. run_phase: the only time consuming phase; drive, monitor, and sequence here under objections.
6. extract_phase: pull data out of monitors and scoreboards while the design state is still fresh.
7. check_phase: compare expected vs actual; decide pass or fail here.
8. report_phase: print the summary of what the test found.
problems.details: UVM runs every test through the same ordered phases, and each phase has a defined job. Build creates components top down and reads the config db. Connect wires the TLM ports bottom up, after every component exists. End of elaboration does final tuning like printing the topology. Start of simulation sets last minute knobs before time starts. Run is the only phase declared as a task, so it is the only one that consumes simulation time; stimulus, driving, and monitoring all happen here under objections. Extract pulls data out of scoreboards and coverage, check compares expected vs actual and decides pass or fail, and report prints the summary. This problem asks for the eight phases in order with one line each on what belongs there.
problems.example:
build_phase   -> create components, read config db
connect_phase -> drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export)
end_of_elaboration_phase -> print topology, final tuning
start_of_simulation_phase -> set final knobs
run_phase     -> drive, monitor, sequence under objections
extract_phase  -> pull counters out of scoreboards
check_phase   -> compare expected vs actual, pass or fail
report_phase  -> print the summary

WRONG variant: connecting drv.seq_item_port to sqr.seq_item_export inside build_phase.
This is wrong because build runs top down: when the env builds, the agent and its children may not exist yet, so the handles are null and the connect crashes. Connect exists precisely because it runs after every build is done.
constraints: Eight phases, in execution order.
One line per phase.
run_phase is the only time consuming phase.
Order matters: build before connect before run.

choices: Build runs top down, so children may not exist yet when a parent builds; connect runs after all builds
It is just a naming convention
quiz.q: Why must TLM connections happen in connect_phase and not build_phase?
quiz.why: Build creates components top down: a parent's build runs before its children's. Connections reference children on both ends, so they must wait until every component exists, which is what connect_phase guarantees.

quiz.q: Which phase decides pass or fail?
quiz.why: Per the key points, check_phase compares expected vs actual and decides pass or fail. report_phase only prints the summary.

choices: It is the only phase that consumes simulation time
quiz.q: Why is run_phase the only phase declared as a task instead of a function?
quiz.why: Functions execute in zero simulation time. Driving pins, waiting for handshakes, and sequencing all need time to pass, so run_phase must be a task.

hints: Order the phases by what they need: you cannot connect what does not exist, and you cannot check before you run.
Build is top down, connect is bottom up. That ordering is the whole reason the two phases are separate.
Only one phase moves time forward. Everything with waits, clocks, or handshakes lives there.
problems.takeaway: The eight phases run in a fixed order where each step depends on the last: build top down, connect after everything exists, run as the only time consuming phase, then extract, check, and report.

problems.title: Full agent
problems.statement: Assemble a complete agent from a sequencer, driver, and monitor. It needs an is_active knob: in active mode it builds all three, in passive mode only the monitor. Connect the driver seq_item_port to the sequencer seq_item_export in the connect phase. The agent is the reusable unit on a real project. I write an agent once for an interface and drop it into the block level env, the subsystem env, and the chip level env. At chip level some interfaces are driven by other blocks or the CPU, so flipping those agents to passive is how you avoid two drivers fighting over the same bus.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Declare uvm_active_passive_enum is_active, default UVM_ACTIVE, settable through the config db.
2. In build_phase always create the monitor; create the sequencer and driver only when is_active == UVM_ACTIVE.
3. In connect_phase: drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export).
4. Pass the virtual interface down to the driver and monitor through the config db.
5. Passive agents exist for interfaces the testbench observes but never drives.
problems.details: The agent is the reusable unit for one interface: a sequencer, driver, and monitor bundled with an is_active knob. In active mode all three are built and the driver is wired to the sequencer; in passive mode only the monitor is built, for interfaces the testbench observes but never drives. The is_active value is typically read from the config db in build_phase so the test can select the mode per agent. The connect phase wires drv.seq_item_port to sqr.seq_item_export, and the virtual interface is passed down through the config db to the driver and monitor. Agents are what make a testbench reusable: the same agent drops into block level and chip level environments unchanged.
problems.example:
is_active=UVM_ACTIVE  -> sequencer + driver + monitor built
is_active=UVM_PASSIVE -> monitor only
connect: drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export)

WRONG variant: the connect call is placed in build_phase instead of connect_phase.
This is wrong because in build the agent builds its children top down, so sqr or drv may still be null when the connect executes. The result is a null handle crash during build, far from the real mistake. Connect exists to run after every component is built.
constraints: is_active defaults to UVM_ACTIVE.
Monitor is always built; sequencer and driver only when active.
Driver to sequencer wiring in connect_phase.
Interface passed via config db.

choices: For an interface the testbench observes but never drives
To make the test run faster
quiz.q: When would you set an agent to UVM_PASSIVE?
quiz.why: Per the key points, passive agents exist for interfaces the testbench observes but never drives: only the monitor is built, no sequencer or driver.

choices: Wires the driver to the sequencer so items flow from sequences to pins
Connects the monitor to the scoreboard
quiz.q: What does drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export) do?
quiz.why: The driver's seq_item_port is how it pulls items; the sequencer's seq_item_export is how it serves them. Connecting the two completes the path from sequence to driver.

choices: UVM_PASSIVE, because the CPU subsystem drives that bus and the testbench only observes
UVM_ACTIVE, because active mode is the default
UVM_PASSIVE for the data agent too
quiz.q: You reuse a block level agent at chip level, where the config bus is now driven by the on chip CPU. Which mode do you pick for that agent?
quiz.why: The testbench must not fight the CPU for the bus. Passive mode builds only the monitor, so the testbench observes the CPU driven traffic without driving it.

hints: Build is conditional on the mode; connect is not. The wiring only makes sense when a driver exists.
Passive mode answers one question: does this testbench drive this interface or only watch it?
The driver to sequencer wiring needs both handles alive, which is exactly what connect_phase guarantees.
problems.takeaway: The agent bundles one interface: active builds sequencer, driver, and monitor, passive builds only the monitor, and the driver to sequencer wiring happens in connect_phase.

problems.title: Scoreboard
problems.statement: Write a scoreboard that subscribes to the monitor transaction stream with a uvm_analysis_imp, compares expected vs actual, counts matches and mismatches, and reports the totals in check_phase. The scoreboard is where bugs get caught on a real project. Every mismatch it reports is either a DUT bug worth filing or a testbench bug worth fixing, and the stashed failing transactions are what make the bug report actionable. I treat the scoreboard as the single source of truth for pass or fail: if the scoreboard is quiet and coverage is complete, I can sign off.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Extend uvm_scoreboard and declare a uvm_analysis_imp #(packet, my_scoreboard).
2. Implement write(packet t): compare each incoming transaction against expected (reference model or second stream).
3. Keep match_count and mismatch_count; stash a few mismatching transactions for debug.
4. In check_phase, raise a uvm_error if mismatch_count > 0 and report both counts.
5. In the env connect_phase: mon.ap.connect(sb.analysis_export).
problems.details: The scoreboard is the checker: it subscribes to the monitor's transaction stream through a uvm_analysis_imp, compares each transaction against expected behavior, and counts matches and mismatches. The imp is parameterized with the transaction type and the scoreboard class, and its write method runs once per published transaction. A few mismatching transactions are stashed for debug so the failure message shows real data, not just a count. In check_phase, after stimulus has ended and the totals are final, it raises a uvm_error if any mismatches were seen and reports both totals. The env wires it up with mon.ap.connect(sb.analysis_export), and the same monitor port can feed a coverage subscriber at the same time.
problems.example:
monitor publishes txn -> sb.write(txn) compares vs expected
match_count=950, mismatch_count=3 -> check_phase raises uvm_error
env connect: mon.ap.connect(sb.analysis_export)

WRONG variant: calling uvm_error inside write() on the first mismatch.
This is wrong because write sees one transaction at a time. A single mismatch is data, not a verdict, and erroring immediately kills the test before the remaining 952 transactions are even checked. Collect first, judge in check_phase when the full picture exists.
constraints: Extends uvm_scoreboard with a uvm_analysis_imp.
write() compares each transaction.
Counters for matches and mismatches.
Verdict in check_phase.

choices: One monitor can broadcast to many subscribers: scoreboard, coverage, checkers
Direct calls are illegal in UVM
quiz.q: Why does the scoreboard use an analysis port instead of a direct method call?
quiz.why: Analysis ports implement a broadcast: the monitor publishes once and every connected imp's write() is called. That lets the scoreboard, coverage collector, and protocol checkers all observe the same stream independently.

choices: write() sees one transaction at a time; the verdict needs the full picture after the run
Counters do not work in write
quiz.q: Why report the verdict in check_phase rather than inside write()?
quiz.why: A single mismatch inside write() is data, not a verdict. check_phase runs after stimulus ends, when the totals are final, so it can report match and mismatch counts and raise the error once.

choices: The monitor port's broadcast mechanism calls it once per published transaction
The driver calls it after item_done
The test calls it in run_phase
quiz.q: The env connects mon.ap to sb.analysis_export. What actually invokes sb.write()?
quiz.why: Writing to an analysis port broadcasts to every connected imp, so each transaction the monitor publishes triggers one write call on the scoreboard automatically.

hints: The scoreboard never touches pins. Its only input is the transaction stream from the monitor.
Think about timing: write runs per transaction during the run, but the verdict needs every transaction. Which phase runs after the run?
One monitor port can feed many subscribers. The scoreboard is just one of them.
problems.takeaway: The scoreboard subscribes to the monitor stream through an analysis imp, compares each transaction, counts results, and delivers the verdict once in check_phase.

problems.title: Base and directed sequences
problems.statement: Write a base sequence class that raises an objection on entry and drops it on exit so tests do not end early. Then write a directed sequence extending it that sends back to back writes followed by reads to the same addresses. On a real project I keep one base sequence with the objection machinery and fifty directed scenarios extending it. Without the base, every scenario duplicates the raise and drop, and sooner or later someone forgets the drop on an early return path and the whole regression hangs at the end of the run. That hang is always misdiagnosed as a DUT problem first.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Base sequence extends uvm_sequence #(packet); raise the objection in pre_body, drop it in post_body.
2. Get the phase handle with get_starting_phase() inside pre_body/post_body.
3. Directed sequence extends the base; in body, use `uvm_do_with for write items, then `uvm_do_with for reads to the same address values.
4. Keep the base generic: objection handling and knobs live there, scenario detail lives in the children.
problems.details: Sequences come in layers. A base sequence class holds the shared machinery: it raises an objection on entry in pre_body and drops it on exit in post_body so the test does not end while stimulus is still running. pre_body and post_body wrap the body automatically, so the drop always executes even if the body takes an early return. The phase handle comes from get_starting_phase, which returns the phase the sequence was started in. Directed sequences extend the base and describe scenarios: back to back writes followed by reads to the same addresses, built with uvm_do_with for inline constraints. The base stays generic; scenario detail lives in the children, so one objection implementation serves every scenario.
problems.example:
base_seq: pre_body raises objection, post_body drops it
wr_then_rd_seq extends base_seq:
  `uvm_do_with(wr, {wr.addr == 8'h10;})
  `uvm_do_with(rd, {rd.addr == 8'h10;})

WRONG variant: the directed sequence raises the objection at the top of body and drops it at the bottom, but the body has an early return on a randomized skip condition.
This is wrong because the early return skips the drop, the objection is never released, and the test hangs at the end of the run waiting for an objection that will never clear. pre_body and post_body exist to make the drop unconditional.
constraints: Base raises objection in pre_body, drops in post_body.
Phase handle from get_starting_phase().
Directed sequences extend the base.
Scenario detail in children, machinery in the base.

choices: The test can end while the sequence is still running
quiz.q: What goes wrong if the objection is never raised?
quiz.why: Objections keep the run phase alive. Without one, the test may finish and tear down while the sequence is mid stimulus, cutting it off.

choices: Every scenario needs it, so it belongs in one shared place
pre_body only exists in base classes
quiz.q: Why put the objection handling in a base sequence instead of each directed sequence?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the base stays generic with objection handling and knobs, while children hold scenario detail. One implementation serves every directed sequence.

choices: The phase the sequence was started in, set by the sequencer
The phase with the most objections
quiz.q: What does get_starting_phase() return in the base sequence?
quiz.why: The sequencer records the phase in which the sequence started. get_starting_phase returns that handle so the objection is raised and dropped on the right phase.

hints: The objection needs to be raised when the sequence starts and dropped when it ends, no matter which path the body takes.
pre_body and post_body wrap the body for you. That wrapping is the fix for the early return bug.
The children should contain only scenario detail. If you see objection code copied into every directed sequence, it belongs in the base.
problems.takeaway: Put objection handling in pre_body and post_body of a base sequence so every directed scenario inherits it and the drop can never be skipped.

problems.title: Factory override
problems.statement: For one specific test, swap in a different driver type using set_type_override_by_type. Write the override call, and explain when you would reach for an instance override instead of a type override. The factory override is how a real project runs a one off variant without forking the testbench. I need an error injecting driver for exactly one test, not a second copy of the whole agent. The override swaps the type for that test only, and everything else stays untouched. The classic mistake is registering it too late and wondering why the test behaved exactly like the passing one.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. In the test build_phase: set_type_override_by_type(my_driver::get_type(), err_driver::get_type()).
2. Every later factory creation of my_driver inside that test returns an err_driver instead.
3. Use instance overrides (set_inst_override_by_type with a hierarchical path) when only one agent of several needs the replacement.
4. Type overrides are blunt: they hit every instance. Prefer instance overrides in multi agent environments.
problems.details: The factory lets one test swap component types without editing the testbench. set_type_override_by_type in the test's build_phase replaces every later creation of my_driver with err_driver: a blunt instrument, useful when the whole test wants the error injecting variant. The override must be registered before the component is created, because the factory consults overrides at creation time and never looks back. When only one agent out of several needs the replacement, reach for an instance override with a hierarchical path instead, via set_inst_override_by_type. The replacement type should extend the original (or share its base) so it still fits the handle the agent holds. In multi agent environments, prefer instance overrides.
constraints: Override registered in the test build_phase.
Type override hits every instance.
Instance override targets one hierarchical path.
Prefer instance overrides with multiple agents.

quiz.q: After set_type_override_by_type(my_driver::get_type(), err_driver::get_type()), what does the factory return for my_driver?
quiz.why: The override tells the factory: whenever my_driver is requested, construct err_driver instead. Every later creation in that test gets the replacement.

choices: When only one agent of several should get the replacement
quiz.q: When is an instance override better than a type override?
quiz.why: Type overrides are blunt: they hit every instance. With several agents, an instance override with a hierarchical path replaces the driver in exactly one of them.

choices: Because the agent holds the driver in a my_driver typed handle, so the replacement must be assignment compatible
Because the factory is slower otherwise
quiz.q: Why should err_driver extend my_driver rather than being an unrelated class?
quiz.why: The agent declares its driver handle as my_driver. An unrelated type would not be assignment compatible, so the build would fail when the factory tries to place it.

hints: Overrides are consulted at creation time. Ask yourself when the driver gets created relative to your override call.
Type overrides are blunt and hit every instance. If you only want one agent changed, you need the path based form.
The replacement must fit where the original sat, so it should extend the original class.
problems.takeaway: Factory overrides swap component types per test without editing the testbench, but they only work if registered before the component is created: type overrides hit every instance, instance overrides target one path.

problems.title: Coverage
problems.statement: Write a covergroup over the transaction addr and data fields with cross coverage between them. Say where you sample it (the monitor is the honest answer) and define what 100 percent means for the key bins. Coverage is the signoff metric on a real project. When my lead asks if we are done, the answer is the coverage report, not a feeling. I write the covergroup from the verification plan, sample it where every transaction is visible, and treat 100 percent with documented waivers as the gate. Anything less is a conversation about risk, not a signoff.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Coverpoints on addr (bins for low, mid, high ranges plus interesting values) and data (bin the ranges; zero is excluded by constraint).
2. Cross addr with data to prove combinations were exercised, not just each field alone.
3. Sample in the monitor write() or in a subscriber on its analysis port, so every observed transaction counts.
4. 100 percent means every bin hit at least once; waive or justify bins the protocol makes unreachable.
5. Tie each bin back to the test plan: bins exist because features exist.
problems.details: Coverage is how you prove the testbench actually exercised the design. This problem builds a covergroup over the transaction addr and data fields: coverpoints bin the interesting ranges, and a cross proves combinations were hit, not just each field alone. It is sampled in the monitor (or a subscriber on its analysis port) so every observed transaction counts, including traffic the DUT generates on its own. 100 percent means every bin hit at least once, with unreachable bins waived and the waiver justified in writing. Every bin traces back to the test plan: a bin nobody can map to a feature is a bin that should not exist.
constraints: Coverpoints on addr and data.
Cross coverage between them.
Sampled in the monitor.
100 percent means every bin hit; justify waivers.

choices: The monitor sees every transaction on the pins, so nothing is missed
Monitors are the only place covergroups compile
quiz.q: Why sample the covergroup in the monitor?
quiz.why: Per the key points, sampling in the monitor (or a subscriber on its analysis port) counts every observed transaction. Sampling in the driver would miss anything the DUT does on its own.

choices: That combinations were exercised, not just each field in isolation
That addr and data are equal
quiz.q: What does the cross between addr and data prove that the coverpoints alone do not?
quiz.why: Individual coverpoints can each hit 100 percent while some addr/data pairs never co occur. The cross requires the combinations themselves to be seen.

choices: Each field was exercised alone, but many combinations never occurred together
The cross is sampled too often
addr and data are uncorrelated by design
quiz.q: Both coverpoints read 100 percent but the addr x data cross sits at 40 percent. What does that tell you?
quiz.why: Full coverpoints only prove each field hit its bins in isolation. The low cross means most combinations never co occurred, which is exactly the gap the cross was built to expose.

hints: Coverage answers one question: did we exercise what the plan said to exercise? Start from the fields the plan cares about.
A cross exists because two coverpoints at 100 percent can still hide untested combinations.
Sample where every transaction is visible. Ask which component sees the pins.
problems.takeaway: Coverage proves the plan was exercised: coverpoints bin the interesting values, crosses prove combinations happened, sample in the monitor, and 100 percent with justified waivers is the signoff gate.

problems.title: Register model
problems.statement: Build a register block with two registers using uvm_reg. Integrate an adapter and a predictor so the model stays in sync with the DUT, then write a frontdoor write/read sequence against it. The register model is how real projects test control and status registers at scale. Firmware style sequences call reg.write and reg.read instead of hand building bus transactions, and the predictor keeps the mirror honest when hardware updates bits on its own. I have debugged failures where the mirror said one thing and the DUT another, and every time the root cause was a missing or miswired predictor, never the DUT.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Extend uvm_reg_block; create two uvm_reg instances, configure them with build() and register them on a map with add_map().
2. Write an adapter extending uvm_reg_adapter: reg2bus and bus2req translate between register ops and bus transactions.
3. Attach a uvm_reg_predictor with its map and adapter so observed bus traffic keeps the mirrored values current.
4. Frontdoor sequence: call reg.write(status, value) and reg.read(status, value) against the default map.
5. On reads, compare mirrored vs actual: a mismatch means the DUT or the adapter is wrong.
problems.details: The register model gives tests a readable, writable mirror of the DUT registers. Build a uvm_reg_block with two registers on an address map: each uvm_reg holds its fields, the map assigns addresses and access policies. An adapter class extending uvm_reg_adapter translates between register operations and bus transactions in both directions: reg2bus turns a reg write into a bus sequence item the driver understands, and bus2reg turns an observed bus transaction back into register data. A uvm_reg_predictor, given the map and the adapter, watches bus traffic on the monitor's analysis port and keeps the mirrored values current, so the mirror stays right even when hardware or another master changes a register. Frontdoor sequences then call reg.write and reg.read against the map and can trust the mirror.
constraints: Two uvm_reg instances on a map.
Adapter translates reg ops to bus txns and back.
Predictor keeps the mirror in sync.
Frontdoor access through the map.

choices: Translate between register operations and bus transactions
quiz.q: What is the adapter's job?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the adapter's reg2bus and bus2req translate register reads/writes into the bus transactions the driver understands, and back.

choices: Bus traffic from other sources would leave the mirror stale
quiz.q: Why attach a predictor instead of updating the mirror only on frontdoor accesses?
quiz.why: The DUT's registers can change from backdoor loads, other masters, or hardware updates. The predictor observes actual bus traffic so the mirrored values stay current.

choices: Frontdoor goes through the bus via the adapter; backdoor pokes the DUT hierarchy directly
quiz.q: What is the difference between a frontdoor and a backdoor register access?
quiz.why: Frontdoor accesses travel the real bus path through the adapter and driver, exercising the design. Backdoor accesses use the HDL path to read or write the register directly, bypassing the bus.

hints: Three pieces work together: the block holds the registers, the adapter speaks the bus, the predictor watches traffic.
The mirror is only trustworthy if something updates it when the test is not the one writing. Ask what that something is.
A register changed by hardware looks identical on the bus to one changed by software. The predictor sees both.
problems.takeaway: The register model mirrors DUT registers: the adapter translates reg ops to bus transactions, the predictor keeps the mirror in sync with real traffic, and frontdoor sequences use the map.

problems.title: Virtual sequencer
problems.statement: Coordinate two agents (config and data) with a virtual sequence running on a virtual sequencer. Explain why the virtual sequencer holds handles to the real sequencers instead of holding sequence items. Multi agent coordination is a daily reality on real projects: program the registers through the config agent, stream packets through the data agent, then check the result, in that order. Without a virtual sequencer each agent runs its own default sequence and the ordering is luck. The virtual sequence is the conductor that makes the two agents play together, and it never touches a sequence item itself.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. The virtual sequencer extends uvm_sequencer and holds handles cfg_sqr and data_sqr, assigned in the env connect_phase.
2. The virtual sequence grabs those handles in pre_body and starts sub sequences on each with `uvm_do_on.
3. The virtual sequencer never sees sequence items, so it is not parameterized on a transaction type.
4. Handles, not items, because its job is coordination: which sub sequencer runs what, and in which order.
problems.details: When a test needs two agents to move in coordination, for example config traffic on one interface and data on another, a virtual sequence conducts them from a virtual sequencer. The virtual sequencer extends uvm_sequencer with no transaction type parameter, because it never handles sequence items; it only holds handles to the real sequencers, assigned in the env's connect_phase after all agents are built. The virtual sequence accesses those handles through p_sequencer, cast to the virtual sequencer type, and launches sub sequences with uvm_do_on against the right handle. Coordination logic, like program the config then stream the data then check the result, lives in the virtual sequence, while the sub sequences stay simple and reusable.
problems.example:
virtual_sequencer: cfg_sqr and data_sqr handles
env connect: vsqr.cfg_sqr = cfg_agent.sqr;
virtual seq: `uvm_do_on(cfg_seq, p_sequencer.cfg_sqr)

WRONG variant: the sequencer handles are assigned in the env's build_phase instead of connect_phase.
This is wrong because build runs top down: when the env builds, the agents have not built their sequencers yet, so cfg_agent.sqr is null and the handle assignment silently stores null. The virtual sequence then fails when it tries to start a sub sequence on a null sequencer. Handles to children are only safe after every build is done.
constraints: Holds handles to the real sequencers.
Not parameterized on a transaction type.
Handles assigned in env connect_phase.
Sub sequences start with uvm_do_on.

choices: It never handles sequence items; it only coordinates sub sequencers
It handles all types at once
quiz.q: Why is the virtual sequencer not parameterized on a transaction type?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the virtual sequencer never sees items, so there is no transaction type to parameterize. Its job is coordination: which sub sequencer runs what, in which order.

quiz.q: Where do the sequencer handles get assigned?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the handles are assigned in the env connect_phase, after all agents (and their sequencers) have been built.

choices: Through p_sequencer, cast to the virtual sequencer type, selecting the target handle with uvm_do_on
It guesses from the sequence name
quiz.q: How does the virtual sequence choose which sequencer a sub sequence runs on?
quiz.why: p_sequencer gives the virtual sequence access to the virtual sequencer's handles, and uvm_do_on starts the sub sequence on the chosen one, like cfg_sqr or data_sqr.

hints: The virtual sequencer is a conductor, not a musician. It holds no items and plays no pins.
The handles point at children of the agents. Ask which phase guarantees those children exist.
Sub sequences launch against a specific handle. The virtual sequence picks which one, and in what order.
problems.takeaway: The virtual sequencer coordinates sub sequencers through handles assigned in the env connect_phase: it holds no items, only references, and the virtual sequence conducts them with uvm_do_on.

problems.title: Layered sequences
problems.statement: Write a higher level scenario sequence that calls lower level read/write sequences instead of raw items. Discuss why this layering lets the same scenario sequences run at both block level and chip level. Layered sequences are how real projects reuse stimulus across the hierarchy. I write boot, traffic, and drain scenarios once at block level, and when the block drops into the chip, the same scenarios run because only the low layer bus sequences get rebound to the chip level sequencer. The day someone writes a scenario that drives raw items directly is the day we maintain two copies of every test.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Low layer: read_seq and write_seq each produce a single bus transaction.
2. High layer: scenario_seq starts the low layer sequences in order, e.g. configure, then traffic, then drain.
3. The scenario never touches pins or raw items, so it does not care what sits underneath.
4. Reuse: at chip level the same scenario runs unchanged once the low layer sequences are rebound to the chip level sequencer.
problems.details: Layered sequences separate what the scenario does from how the bus wiggles. The low layer has small sequences like read_seq and write_seq, each producing a single bus transaction and knowing the protocol details. The high layer has scenario sequences that call the low layer ones in order: configure, then traffic, then drain. Because the scenario never touches pins or raw items, the same scenario runs unchanged at block level and at chip level once the low layer sequences are rebound to the chip level sequencer. The rebinding happens below the scenario: the low layer sequences are started on the new sequencer, and the scenario code does not change at all.
problems.example:
low:  write_seq -> one bus write ; read_seq -> one bus read
high: scenario_seq: write_seq x N, then read_seq x N
same scenario_seq runs at block and chip level

WRONG variant: the scenario sequence creates raw bus items directly and calls start_item and finish_item on the block level sequencer.
This is wrong because the scenario is now welded to one sequencer and one item type. At chip level, where the bus topology is different, the scenario no longer compiles or drives the wrong interface. The whole point of layering is that the scenario only speaks the low layer's language, never the bus's.
constraints: Low layer: single transaction sequences.
High layer: scenarios calling low layer sequences.
Scenarios never touch pins or raw items.
Reuse across block and chip level.

choices: It never touches pins or raw items, only the low layer sequences
quiz.q: What makes the same scenario sequence reusable at chip level?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the scenario only calls low layer sequences. Rebinding those low layer sequences to the chip level sequencer moves the whole scenario up a level unchanged.

choices: In the low layer sequences and the driver, not in the scenario
quiz.q: In this layering, where does protocol detail (like the valid/ready handshake) live?
quiz.why: The low layer produces bus transactions and the driver turns them into pin wiggles. The scenario stays at the 'what', the lower layers handle the 'how'.

choices: Nothing; the low layer sequences are started on the new sequencer and the scenario is untouched
The scenario is rewritten for the chip level bus
quiz.q: At chip level the low layer write_seq targets a different sequencer. What changes in the scenario sequence?
quiz.why: Rebinding happens in the layer below the scenario. The scenario still just calls write_seq; only where write_seq runs has changed.

hints: Two layers, two vocabularies: the low layer speaks bus transactions, the high layer speaks scenarios.
Ask what the scenario sequence is allowed to touch. If the answer includes pins or raw items, the layering is broken.
Reuse across levels works because only the bottom layer gets rebound. The scenario above it never notices.
problems.takeaway: Layered sequences separate intent from mechanism: scenarios call low layer bus sequences, never pins or raw items, so rebinding the low layer moves the scenario from block to chip level unchanged.

problems.title: Error injection
problems.statement: Write a sequence that injects parity errors into the data stream. The scoreboard must flag the corrupted transactions, and an interface assertion must still prove the protocol itself stayed legal while errors were being injected. Error injection is a signoff activity on real projects: you have to prove the DUT detects and handles bad data, not just good data. I inject at a controlled rate, account for every injected error in the scoreboard as expected, and keep the protocol assertions running throughout. The day the scoreboard cannot tell an injected error from a real bug is the day the test stops meaning anything.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. The error sequence extends the normal data sequence and flips parity bits on chosen items (constrain when errors happen).
2. The scoreboard compares against expected data and counts parity mismatches as expected errors, not DUT bugs.
3. A concurrent interface assertion checks the valid/ready rules still hold during injection.
4. This separates data integrity checking from protocol checking: both must pass, independently.
problems.details: Error injection proves the testbench checks data integrity without confusing it with protocol correctness. An error sequence extends the normal data sequence and flips parity bits on chosen items, constrained so errors happen where the test wants them at a controlled rate. The scoreboard compares against expected data and counts the parity mismatches as expected errors, not DUT bugs: the check is that the DUT detected and flagged them, not that the data arrived clean. Meanwhile a concurrent interface assertion proves the valid/ready protocol stayed legal throughout the injection, because corrupt data must never come with a broken handshake. Data integrity and protocol legality are checked independently, and both must pass.
problems.example:
err_seq extends data_seq: flips parity on every 10th item
scoreboard: parity mismatches counted as expected errors
assertion: valid/ready rules hold during the whole run

WRONG variant: the scoreboard has no expected error accounting, so every injected parity mismatch is reported as a DUT bug.
This is wrong because the test itself corrupted the data on purpose. Failing the DUT for detecting exactly what you injected makes the test useless: it can never pass, and the real signal, whether the DUT flagged the error correctly, is buried under false failures.
constraints: Error sequence extends the normal sequence.
Scoreboard treats injected errors as expected.
Interface assertion checks protocol during injection.
Data integrity and protocol checked independently.

choices: The errors were deliberately injected, so flagging them as DUT bugs would be wrong
quiz.q: Why must the scoreboard treat injected parity errors as expected?
quiz.why: Per the key points, the scoreboard counts parity mismatches as expected errors. The test put them there on purpose; the check is that they are detected, not that they never happen.

choices: To prove the protocol stayed legal even while data was being corrupted
The scoreboard cannot run during injection
quiz.q: Why keep a separate interface assertion running during error injection?
quiz.why: Per the key points, this separates data integrity checking from protocol checking. Corrupt data must never come with a broken handshake.

choices: Uncontrolled errors are unreproducible and can push the DUT outside the intended scenario
quiz.q: Why constrain the error rate instead of leaving corruption fully random?
quiz.why: A controlled rate keeps the test reproducible and the DUT inside the scenario being verified. Fully random corruption makes failures impossible to reproduce and debug.

hints: Two things are under test at once: did the data get corrupted as planned, and did the protocol stay legal?
The scoreboard needs to know which errors were injected. An unexpected mismatch and an expected one must be counted differently.
The error rate is a knob, not an accident. Fully random corruption is unreproducible and drowns the scenario.
problems.takeaway: Error injection tests data integrity and protocol independently: inject at a controlled rate, count injected errors as expected in the scoreboard, and keep interface assertions proving the handshake stayed legal.

problems.title: Verification plan to closure
problems.statement: From a feature list to a coverage model to a test list: write a mini verification plan for a synchronous FIFO. Define the coverage closure criteria: what has to be true before you can call the FIFO verified. The verification plan is the contract I sign with my lead on a real project. It answers the only question that matters at the end: are we done. Features become coverage bins, bins become tests, and closure is four gates with artifacts behind each one. I have watched projects declare victory on a green regression with 60 percent coverage, and every one of them found the missing bugs after tapeout instead of before.
problems.solution:
Key points:
1. Feature list: push, pop, full, empty, almost full, simultaneous push and pop, reset behavior.
2. Coverage model: coverpoints on occupancy, flags, and pointer crossings, with crosses between them.
3. Test list: directed tests per feature plus constrained random with knobs for depth pressure.
4. Closure criteria: 100 percent of planned bins hit, all assertions passing with no open waivers, every test green on the final regression, and every bug fixed and re verified.
problems.details: A verification plan turns 'test the FIFO' into an executable contract. Start from the feature list: push, pop, full, empty, almost full, simultaneous push and pop, reset behavior. Build a coverage model with coverpoints on occupancy, flags, and pointer crossings, crossed between them, so combinations like push and pop at full are proven, not assumed. Write the test list: directed tests per feature plus constrained random with knobs for depth pressure. Closure has four gates: 100 percent of planned bins hit, all assertions passing with no open waivers, every test green on the final regression, and every bug fixed and re verified. A gate is not met by a feeling; each one has an artifact: the coverage report, the waiver log, the regression results, and the bug tracker.
problems.example:
feature: simultaneous push+pop at full
cover: cross occupancy x push x pop
test:  directed_push_pop_full + random depth_pressure
closure: bins 100%, assertions clean, regression green, bugs closed

WRONG variant: declaring the FIFO verified because every test passes, while coverage sits at 60 percent and two assertion waivers are undocumented.
This is wrong because passing tests only prove the scenarios you wrote. Without the coverage bins there is no proof the features were exercised, and undocumented waivers hide exactly the checks that were skipped. A green regression with holes in coverage is not signoff, it is risk you have not measured.
constraints: Feature list first.
Coverage model with crosses.
Directed plus constrained random tests.
Four closure gates.

choices: 100 percent of planned bins hit with no open assertion waivers
quiz.q: Which of these is a closure criterion from the plan?
quiz.why: Per the key points, closure needs: 100 percent of planned bins hit, all assertions passing with no open waivers, every test green on the final regression, and every bug fixed and re verified.

choices: Directed tests hit known corner cases; random explores the space between them
The plan requires exactly two tests
quiz.q: Why include both directed tests and constrained random in the test list?
quiz.why: Directed tests target specific features like simultaneous push and pop at full. Constrained random with depth pressure knobs covers the combinations nobody thought to direct.

choices: No; coverage is the proof the feature was exercised, and without bins the gate is not met
Yes, if the waveform looked right
No, because random tests are missing
quiz.q: A feature has passing tests but zero coverage bins. Per the plan, is it verified?
quiz.why: Tests without coverage prove only that the written scenarios ran. The coverage model is the contract for what exercised means, so missing bins mean the feature is not closed.

hints: The plan flows in one direction: features define coverage, coverage defines tests, tests produce the closure evidence.
Each closure gate needs an artifact you can point at. If you cannot show it, the gate is not met.
Directed tests and random tests do different jobs. Ask which one finds the corner case you already know about, and which one finds the one you did not.
problems.takeaway: A verification plan turns features into coverage bins into tests, and closure means four proven gates: full bins, clean assertions, green regression, closed bugs.
